entry.heading: Chainsaw Man (Tatsuki Fujimoto)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life here is an ordinary one: food, a home, people to eat with, and the freedom to choose your own wants instead of having them chosen for you.

frames.aligns: Care for the poor; human dignity against being used as a tool; sacrificial love among friends; manipulation exposed as evil.
frames.concerns: Devil contracts as normal; lust as a hero's motive without much judgment; cannibalism framed as "love" (ch. 96-97). Fantasy demons are judged by framing (CCC 2115-2117), so some parents allow it for older teens.

frames.aligns: Evil is real and deceptive; Makima as a false shepherd; grief that leads to care.
frames.concerns: Demons are taken as real, so a devil-hybrid hero and friendly devils conflict with teaching throughout; passions fed rather than resisted. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the imagery itself a serious concern.

frames.aligns: Sin has consequences; manipulation is exposed; loyalty and care for a child.
frames.concerns: Devils as friends; lust as motive; alcohol use by minors (many Baptists are teetotal). Views vary by congregation; Plugged In, widely used by Baptists, rated the film "Heavy" for all ages.

frames.aligns: Evil disguised as good (Makima); found family; a story some Christians use to talk about young men's brokenness (Beneath the Tangles).
frames.concerns: Demonic content in a heroic frame; lust as the main motive. Churches range from avoiding it to discussing it with older teens.

frames.aligns: Spiritual deception and bondage shown as real harms; freedom from control.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": devils, contracts, Hell and a hero fused with a devil are central and treated as normal or good throughout.

frames.aligns: Total depravity is vivid; common grace lets some readers value its honesty about desire and abuse.
frames.concerns: Suicide as self-murder (WLC Q136) used as a plot twist; occult framing; lust largely unjudged.

frames.aligns: Law and gospel themes: Denji cannot save himself; grace-like gifts come through others; misuse of authority exposed.
frames.concerns: Devils normalized; sexual ethics (sixth commandment). LCMS and ELCA families may differ on how much to allow.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace echoes in small mercies; social holiness critique of exploitation.
frames.concerns: Holiness emphasis on purity; underage drinking against historic abstinence. Holiness churches stricter than UMC.

frames.aligns: Imaginative tradition (C.S. Lewis) gives room for dark fantasy judged by framing; critique of misused power.
frames.concerns: Devils normalized; chastity themes. Episcopal and ACNA families may differ.

frames.aligns: Critique of state violence and of using people as weapons.
frames.concerns: Violence shown as heroic spectacle is the central concern, and it is the story's engine; sexual content. Progressive Mennonites may engage it as critique; conservative groups would avoid it.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, care for a child, warnings about manipulation.
frames.concerns: Casual sexual ethics; alcohol (Word of Wisdom); devils as companions.

frames.aligns: Care for the vulnerable; exposure of deception.
frames.concerns: Devils and Hell treated as everyday; impure content against Fundamental Belief 22.
Demon contact, immorality and violence (Psalm 11:5; Galatians 5:19-21) are woven through and shown as normal for the hero.

frames.aligns: Freedom from control; love expressed in small kindnesses.
frames.concerns: Fear itself is the devils' power source, and the story dwells on fear, sin and bodily harm.

frames.aligns: Critique of exploited labor, poverty and state power; sympathy for an abused youth; LGBTQ side characters.
frames.concerns: Consent issues (ch. 132, 136, 167-168); sexualized teens; Denji's homophobia in Part 1 (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Respect for life shown through grief; critique of tyranny; truth about abuse.
frames.concerns: Devils normalized (Deuteronomy 18); lust as motive; Makima's claim that devils erased the Holocaust from history (ch. 84). Tzniut and nivul peh make the depiction a serious concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Critique of tyranny and exploitation; grief and care.
frames.concerns: Casual sexual ethics; the Holocaust line (ch. 84), spoken by the villain, may need discussion.

frames.aligns: Social critique of exploitation; tikkun olam echoes in caring for Nayuta. No antisemitic tropes found.
frames.concerns: Consent; the Holocaust line (ch. 84) in a villain's mouth.

frames.aligns: Mercy to orphans and animals; warnings against arrogance and control over others.
frames.concerns: Devils (shayatin) as partners and pets; lust and alcohol treated as normal. Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) makes the nudity a serious concern.

frames.aligns: Desire and suffering; rebirth of devils; dharma-like duty in Aki.
frames.concerns: The absence of the sacred; a Hindu traditionalist essay calls Denji nihilistic and Makima "desacralizing" femininity, while praising Aki and Himeno (cshc Substack).

frames.aligns: Craving as the root of suffering, shown as what gets Denji used; impermanence; endless rebirth of devils looks like samsara (our framing).
frames.concerns: Appetite treated as a hero's fuel; killing constant (first precept).

frames.aligns: Sincerity in Denji; gratitude for small things (bread, a bed).
frames.concerns: Death, blood and impurity everywhere with no purification; little sacred framing.

frames.aligns: Care for the vulnerable; honest work valued.
frames.concerns: Lust (kaam), one of the five vices, is the hero's open and sympathetic motive.

frames.aligns: Critique of domination; service in small acts.
frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's warning against degrading art and entertainment applies to the sexual content and its framing.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: care for children, honesty; critique of control and manipulation.
frames.concerns: Casual cruelty and killing ("do not murder").
"Harm none" against constant harm; consent violations (sex is sacred between consenting adults).

frames.aligns: Critique of labor exploitation, poverty and state power; Asa as an honest portrait of an awkward girl (Kotaku); platonic Denji-Power bond (Anime Feminist).
frames.concerns: Sexualization of 16-year-old characters; consent (ch. 132, 136, 167-168); Power's trauma used for Denji's growth (Anime Feminist); suicide safe-messaging.

frames.aligns: This-life meaning through friends, meals and care; no supernatural rescue; critical view of authority; nihilism explored but small joys kept.
Strong warnings about manipulation; value of home, meals and work; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Absent and abusive fathers; crude sexuality; nihilism; cult imagery; anti-authority tone.

frames.aligns: Rejection of control by authority; the right to choose one's own desires (Church of Satan's indulgence; Satanic Temple's bodily autonomy).
frames.concerns: Harm to children and animals (Nayuta, the dogs), though done by villains; consent violations against Denji.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of an exploited youth; justice against exploitation.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Aki's duty-and-revenge path ends with him turned into the Gun Fiend (ch. 79). Denji's answer to Makima is not vengeance but eating her as "love" and raising Nayuta (ch. 96-97).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Total control is the villain's creed (Makima's "better world," ch. 84). The good is choosing your own wants instead of having them handed to you as a leash (Philosophy essay; life message). Public Safety treats workers as expendable.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family carries the warmth: Aki, Power and Denji's shared home, and later Nayuta (ch. 232). Wider institutions and crowds (the Chainsaw Man Church, ch. 140) appear as threats.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Those who seek control lose (Makima, Barem, Yoru). The state and cynical veterans are critiqued (Kishibe). Authority appears mostly as exploitation.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion is imagery and a student cult, not living faith; there is no God figure. Salvation-like moments come through human love and a shared meal (Religious lens).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Denji's dreams are basic: jam on bread, a warm bed, a girlfriend (ch. 1). Poverty and child debt frame the story. The goal of choosing one's own desires pulls the position slightly up.

folkways.japan: Public Safety's disposable workers and "death as a workplace hazard" echo critiques of Japanese overwork culture rather than the story's own message, and Part 2's fame culture and hero worship reflect Japanese online and idol culture.

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Its ideas come through absurd, violent events and the characters' choices rather than stated morals.

personified.ideology: A better world through total control
Simple desires and living day to day

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Absurdism, Pagan/occult imagery, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Hedonism (explored).

entry.heading: Jujutsu Kaisen (Gege Akutami)
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Self-giving love: Yuji, Nanami and Gojo give their lives for others. Yuji refuses to treat anyone as disposable. Cruelty and nihilism are defeated.
frames.concerns: Fantasy magic is judged by framing, and here sorcery, summoning and possession are the heroes' craft (CCC 2115-2117); a cult cheers a child's death; Mei Mei goes unpunished.

frames.aligns: Struggle against evil; repentance-like grief after Shibuya (ch. 127); honor for the dead.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real, so demon-like curses and possession used as a skill system turn spiritual warfare into a tool. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore itself a concern.

frames.aligns: Responsibility after failure; courage; loyalty; Yuji's refusal to abandon others.
frames.concerns: Sorcery, summoning and spirits as the heroes' tools (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); self-harm (Toji). Views vary by congregation because each church is self-governing; some families accept fantasy magic, many are cautious with spells and spirits.

frames.aligns: Clear evil fought at cost; mentors who sacrifice; the Higuruma arc read as human justice failing and grace needed (Beneath the Tangles).
frames.concerns: Occult mechanics and possession; despair. Range is wide: some churches treat the magic like Tolkien-style fantasy, others avoid spirit-contact stories entirely.

frames.aligns: Courage and self-sacrifice; evil is real and must be fought.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": curses, possession, body-stealing and summoned spirits are the engine of the story and the heroes' means. Demon-like villains are fan favorites.

frames.aligns: Total depravity is vivid: every institution and most adults fail. Common grace: self-sacrifice and loyalty still shine.
frames.concerns: Occult framework; suicide (WLC Q136 calls it self-murder, handled pastorally).

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: the story is heavy on law (judgment, guilt, Higuruma's court) and shows grace mainly as forgiveness between brothers (Yuji and Choso).
frames.concerns: Occult themes (Large Catechism on misuse of God's name includes sorcery). LCMS and WELS families tend to be stricter than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace-like moments: Yuji keeps choosing to help after failing. Social holiness: reform of an unjust system.
frames.concerns: Occult; holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Sacrifice and duty; grief and remembrance; works judged by how they frame good and evil, in a fantasy tradition with deep Anglican roots (C.S. Lewis).
frames.concerns: Occult system; bleak afterlife. Episcopal families generally less concerned than ACNA families.

frames.aligns: Mutual care; refusal to treat anyone as disposable; humility (Yuji as one "cog").
frames.concerns: Violence shown as heroic is the central concern, and the series is built on it (Matthew 5:39); occult themes. Conservative groups avoid most popular media; MC USA families are more varied.

frames.aligns: Family-like loyalty; sacrifice; repentance after failure.
frames.concerns: Spirit contact and summoning as heroic tools; a bleak afterlife; Mei Mei material.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice; responsibility; care for the weak.
frames.concerns: Spiritualism is rejected, and here spirits, a seance revival (Toji, ch. 113) and afterlife scenes are shown as real.

frames.aligns: Love among friends; honesty about failure.
frames.concerns: Spiritism, magic and spirit contact are the core of the story and the heroes' craft (Galatians 5:19-21); fighting as the hero's calling.

frames.aligns: Curses born of human fear and hatred echo the teaching that thought shapes experience; love and cooperation win.
frames.concerns: Evil, fear and death are shown as real, overwhelming forces; despair.

frames.aligns: Justice themes: corrupt elders, a failed court (Higuruma), inherited privilege, Maki against a sexist clan.
frames.concerns: Critics' view that women are sidelined (ANN review); Mei Mei material and consent.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh-like ethic: Yuji acts to save lives. Memory of the dead is central.
frames.concerns: Sorcery (Deuteronomy 18) presented as a legitimate craft; suicide. Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Saving life; memory of the dead; justice against a corrupt elite.
frames.concerns: Sorcery as a craft, though many families accept fantasy; suicide; Mei Mei material.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: reform of a closed elite; Higuruma's critique of the courts; human dignity.
Courage, protecting the weak, patience (sabr), justice against corrupt elders.
frames.concerns: Sihr (sorcery) and spirit summoning are the heroes' core craft; possession and body-theft; Mei Mei material.

frames.aligns: Dharma-like duty to fight to protect others; karma-like consequences for cruelty; mudras and Buddhist-derived imagery treated as powerful.
frames.concerns: Sacred imagery used for spectacle; some apply the Gita's tamasic category to the gore.

frames.aligns: Many Buddhist motifs: suffering born of negative emotion (curses), impermanence, mudras. Yuji's acceptance that he is one part of a larger whole echoes non-self. Pride ("I alone am the honored one") is shown as isolating.
frames.concerns: Buddhist imagery is used for battle and spectacle; the first precept is rarely discussed.

frames.aligns: Folk spirits (yokai, onryo) familiar from Japanese culture; purification and barriers echo shrine practice.
frames.concerns: A shrine image as a killing domain (Sukuna's Malevolent Shrine); kami-like beings used as weapons.

frames.aligns: Courage to defend the oppressed; ego, anger and lust (Sukuna's appetite) shown as destructive and defeated.
Service and self-sacrifice; unity of a group over the lone strongest.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence; spirit contact; Mei Mei material.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: help others, do not murder (murderers are defeated).
frames.concerns: Despair and trauma themes, which the Church reads apart from psychiatry.

frames.aligns: Sorcerers shown as heroes rather than stereotyped; responsibility for one's power.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" set against constant killing; Mei Mei material.

frames.aligns: Critique of a closed, aging elite and inherited privilege; Maki against a misogynist clan; Higuruma's critique of the courts.
frames.concerns: Critics argue women are sidelined in the second half (Nobara absent from ch. 125 to ch. 267). Mei Mei / Ui Ui framing and consent. Suicide shown on page (safe-messaging concern).

frames.aligns: Yuji's ethic rests on human dignity and care, not divine command; the strongest and the cruelest lose to cooperation; nihilism answered. Magic is clearly fiction.
frames.concerns: Despair and suicide content for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Duty, sacrifice, loyalty, honor, respect for good mentors (Nanami, Yaga). Clear villains. Responsibility for consequences.
frames.concerns: Authority and tradition are almost always shown as corrupt; fan culture celebrating Sukuna.

frames.aligns: Challenges arbitrary authority (the higher-ups); compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2); no divine command.
frames.concerns: The ethic is group over self; harm to children (Riko, Tsumiki) and Mei Mei's treatment of her brother.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every life (Yuji); justice and reform of a corrupt system.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge appears often (Junpei, ch. 19-27; Maki's destruction of the Zenin clan, ch. 149-151) but is not the story's answer; Yuji's creed is to help people and accept being one "cog" (ch. 127 onward).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The closed, aging elite and its execution orders are critiqued, yet Yuji's "cog" ethic and Nanami's adult duty (ch. 120) honor doing one's part inside a team.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Every life counts (Yuji's grandfather, ch. 1). Clan and blood ties are mostly harmful: the Zenin reject children without techniques, Kenjaku poses as Yuji's "mother" (ch. 143).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The higher-ups and clan elders are discredited; the strongest individual (Sukuna) is defeated by a team (ch. 268). Gojo's turn from "honored one" to teacher is the story's answer to rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Buddhist and Shinto imagery is respected as beauty and power, but tradition is mostly shown as violent and the cult that applauds Riko's death (ch. 72-76) is condemned. Secular humanism through Yuji gets the last word.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Death is certain and sudden; the life message is to help others and die without regret. Survival of the group against curses dominates over personal fulfillment.

folkways.japan: Sorcerer clans, an elder council and school-based teams reflect Japanese clan and senpai-kohai structures the story largely critiques; Nanami's dislike of overwork comments on Japanese salaryman culture.

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Rival philosophies are voiced by antagonists in battle dialogue, while Yuji answers them by action rather than argument.

personified.ideology: Strength and pleasure are all that matter
Souls are only shapes; nothing has meaning

entry.dominant: Dharmic (Buddhist) imagery, Pagan/occult (Japanese folk religion), Existentialism, Might makes right (critiqued), Nihilism (critiqued). The labels below are this entry's framing unless a source is named.

entry.heading: Berserk
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a stubborn struggle: you keep fighting against fate, cruelty and your own rage, and you choose to protect the people beside you rather than sacrifice them for a dream.

content.framing: Mixed: sexual violence shown as atrocity with lasting consequences; critics dispute how it is drawn

frames.aligns: Dignity of victims; evil framed as evil; Guts's turn from vengeance to protection; pride and the "sale of the soul" (Griffith) end in monstrousness; Griffith as a false messiah.
frames.concerns: Inter Mirifica 7 accepts depicting evil when it is not made attractive; critics' charge that the rape is drawn as spectacle bears on that. The Holy See and inquisition as persecutors may read as aimed at the Church. Witchcraft is shown as good. Explicit rape and nudity (CCC 2354, 2521-2524) are a depiction matter.

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions: Guts's "inner Beast" as a picture of wrath; Griffith's pride; a false savior exposed.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real, so a story where demonic power wins and witchcraft heals is a spiritual concern at the level of message; the church shown as cruel. Watchfulness over what one looks at (nepsis) makes the explicit imagery a heavy concern apart from message.

frames.aligns: Clear evil in the God Hand; consequences for betrayal; fellowship and protection in the later arcs.
frames.concerns: Witchcraft shown as wise and good (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); a corrupt church; revenge as the main motive for many volumes. Explicit sexual content, gore and profanity weigh heavily under Philippians 4:8. Each congregation is self-governing, so views vary.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles reads Guts's arc as moving toward "restored faith instead of bitter distrust" and fellowship (Hebrews 12:24). Many in this tradition distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it, and Berserk condemns what it shows.
frames.concerns: Positive witchcraft; a corrupt church; a hope that is human rather than Christian. Some families favor separation from such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Spiritual warfare imagery: a real fight against demonic powers that are shown as evil.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": demonic sacrifice, cursed brands, spirit contact and witchcraft taught as good are a message issue here, not only imagery. The story places the origin of evil in human minds (Idea of Evil) rather than in a spiritual enemy.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has a strong echo: human sin produces the Idea of Evil and the apostles. Common grace lets adults value serious art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: A fatalistic "causality" in place of providence; the church shown as cruel; positive witchcraft. WLC Q139 lists lascivious books and pictures, so the explicit sexual imagery is a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: no character can save himself; the story shows the bondage of the will and works-righteousness (Griffith's dream) ending in ruin.
frames.concerns: No gospel offered; witchcraft and demonic pacts. Entertainment is adiaphora, judged by conscience; LCMS and WELS families are more cautious than ELCA about the explicitness.

frames.aligns: Holiness of care: the later arcs center caring for a wounded woman; social holiness toward refugees and the poor at Albion.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus"; occult shown as good; revenge. Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) are far more cautious than UMC about the explicitness.

frames.aligns: A tradition of dark fantasy and moral seriousness (Lewis, Tolkien, Sayers) that judges works by how they frame good and evil; Berserk frames its atrocities as evil.
frames.concerns: The church as persecutor; witchcraft as good; the world's reward of Griffith. Episcopal and ACNA families both likely to treat the explicitness as adult reading.

frames.aligns: Mercy toward the wounded; a small caring community; violence shown as a cycle that consumes everyone.
frames.concerns: Violence shown as heroic is the central concern: the sword is the story's engine and its answer, even after Guts turns to protecting others (Matthew 5:39). Old Order groups avoid such media entirely; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family-like loyalty; healing from trauma; agency against fate.
frames.concerns: Witchcraft as good; a corrupt church; revenge as motive. For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the publisher's 18+ rating and the explicitness put it outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: Care for the wounded; evil shown as destructive.
frames.concerns: Spiritualism and witchcraft shown as wise and healing conflict with Adventist teaching on the state of the dead and spirit contact; revenge. Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" make the explicitness a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Evil shown as evil; protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: jw.org counsel asks whether entertainment features what God hates: violence (Psalm 11:5), immorality and spiritism (Galatians 5:19-21). Here spiritism and magic are shown as good and fighting is the hero's way of life.

frames.aligns: Love and care as what heals Casca; Griffith's material power shown as hollow.
frames.concerns: Evil is presented as a cosmic power (the Idea of Evil, the God Hand), against the teaching that evil has no reality in God's creation; the story dwells on fear, sin and bodily ruin, which members guard thought against ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Critique of religious violence and fanaticism (Mozgus, witch hunts); empathy for refugees and the poor; Casca's recovery through women's care.
frames.concerns: Whether the sexual violence serves victims or exploits them; the "fridging" of Casca and her long silence; Guts as a male abuse survivor needs careful handling.

frames.aligns: Respect for life amid chaos; memory of the dead (the Band); critique of inquisitions and witch hunts, which echo historical persecution of Jews.
frames.concerns: Sorcery shown as wise (Deuteronomy 18:10-11); a cosmic god of evil; revenge as motive (Leviticus 19:18). Tzniut and nivul peh make the explicit sexual content a heavy concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Critique of inquisition and persecution; dignity of victims; revenge shown as consuming.
frames.concerns: Sorcery shown as good (fantasy is generally accepted, sorcery itself is not); a cosmic god of evil. Degrading sexual content is a concern under Jewish values of modesty and dignity.

frames.aligns: Critique of religious fanaticism and persecution; justice for the poor and refugees; care for a survivor.
frames.concerns: Whether the sexual violence is exploitative; women as frequent victims. Fantasy magic is not a concern. Cruelty and exploitation are the ethical tests.

frames.aligns: Patience under trial (sabr); loyalty; protecting the weak; Griffith's pride as ruin.
frames.concerns: Sorcery (sihr) shown as wise and healing; demonic beings given power and worshipped; revenge. "Lowering the gaze" (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes the explicit sexual content and nudity a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Karma-like "causality"; the duty to protect; craving for power as ruin.
frames.concerns: Ganishka transforms into a monstrous form the story calls Shiva (Wikipedia): misuse of a deity's name is the main message concern. Tamasic content under Gita 17 is a depiction matter. Communities vary.

frames.aligns: Suffering, craving and attachment (Griffith's dream, the apostles' trades); the Idea of Evil as born from human minds; Guts's slow release from revenge.
frames.concerns: Revenge as motive for much of the story. Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind makes the explicit killing and sexual violence a heavy concern (first and third precepts).

frames.aligns: Spirits, elves and nature magic treated with respect; loyalty and sincerity; impurity (the Eclipse, the apostles) shown as corrupting.
frames.concerns: No doctrine on fiction and no shrines or kami are mocked. Blood and death are kegare (ritual impurity), so the gore may weigh with some families.

frames.aligns: The five vices shown as destructive: Griffith's ego (haumai), the apostles' lust and greed, Guts's anger as a "Beast"; the saint-soldier ideal in Guts's turn to protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Revenge, not defense of the oppressed, drives much of the fighting. Lust shown so often and so explicitly is a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Service to the weak; care for the traumatized; the cost of pride.
frames.concerns: Revenge and conflict as the main tools; a religion shown mainly as persecutor. Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" makes the explicit sexual content a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Survival and will across the dynamics; care for one's group; Griffith's harm to people of good will condemned. "Do not murder" and "Do not harm a person of good will" (The Way to Happiness) fit the story's verdict on the Eclipse.
frames.concerns: Revenge; glorified violence in places. No content code for fiction.

frames.aligns: Witches (Flora, Schierke) and nature magic shown as wise, healing and persecuted by a fanatic church, the accurate and respectful portrayal this tradition values; a pagan cult around Slan is framed as evil, not as typical paganism.
frames.concerns: The Rede ("harm none") against the story's revenge and constant killing.

frames.aligns: Critique of religious fanaticism and abusive power; the long trauma-recovery arc; a male survivor of child sexual abuse.
frames.concerns: Reliance on sexual violence and Casca's silence for 27 volumes (Anime Feminist; MyAnimeList reviewers); racial depiction debates. Consent, representation and safe messaging make the explicitness a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Human will against an indifferent or hostile cosmos; friendship and care as what gives life meaning; critique of superstition and inquisition.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and exploitation are this tradition's concern: whether the sexual violence is depicted for understanding or for shock.

frames.aligns: Courage, endurance, protective masculinity in Guts's later arcs, loyalty and honor (Zodd, the Skull Knight); the danger of the charismatic leader.
frames.concerns: A corrupt church; anti-authority themes; occult shown as good. Media that degrades the good, the true and the beautiful is a depiction concern. Some conservative commentators praise Guts as a masculine model (Substack essays found, not opened).

frames.aligns: Art that challenges authority is valued: a corrupt church, a false messiah exposed and a hero who defies fate (the "Struggler"). Harm to children and unwanted sexual advances, which the Eleven Rules condemn, are framed as atrocity.
frames.concerns: The God Hand and apostles use demonic imagery as pure evil, a kind of stereotype some Satanists object to, though no Satanists appear.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person, including refugees and heretics; critique of religious persecution; care for a survivor.
frames.concerns: Whether the sexual violence respects or exploits victims; women as frequent victims. Age-appropriateness makes this adult reading.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Guts's blood vow against Griffith after the Eclipse (v12-13) drives the story, and Zodd's warrior honor is admired. The story also shows his rage as dangerous (the "Beast," v23) and gives most hope to his turn from revenge to protecting others (v35-41), which keeps the position below the top.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Institutions are corrupt or helpless: noble courts, the Holy See's Inquisition under Mozgus (Conviction arc, v16-21). Guts lives as a lone mercenary, then with a small free band; no state or church is shown as a source of good order.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty runs to a small chosen band: the Hawks, then Casca, Farnese, Schierke and Isidro. Griffith's crime is betraying that band for personal gain (the Eclipse, v12-13). Wider society barely appears as an object of loyalty.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Noble rank is shown as cruel (rape and torture by nobles; peasants and refugees suffer). Following a leader's dream ends in the Band's sacrifice. Zodd and the Skull Knight are respected for strength, not title.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Organized religion appears mostly as persecution (Mozgus, v16-21), but nature-based witchcraft is shown as wisdom (Flora, Schierke) and fate and causality frame the world (ep. 83). Neither faith nor secular reason is the story's guide.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A world of war, plague and constant random death; strength, skill and willpower keep you alive (Pragmatic lens). The good the story offers is survival and protecting companions, not self-fulfillment.

folkways.japan: The setting is a Japanese reworking of medieval Europe, so its honor code is not a direct mirror of Japanese norms; the master-and-retainer bond inside the Band of the Hawk and the ideas of fate and causality the essay notes echo Japanese storytelling more than the story's own message.

delivery.evidence: A.V. Club (Jones): "It is not concerned with right from wrong." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about struggle, ambition and fate are carried by action and imagery, and the unfinished story gives no final verdict.

personified.ideology: A dream that justifies any sacrifice

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Might makes right (critiqued), Pagan/occult (explored), Nihilism (explored and resisted), Christian (critiqued as institution, echoed in themes).

entry.heading: One Piece
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a free life spent chasing your own dream, side by side with friends who would die for you, and never bowing to anyone who claims the right to own other people.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; condemned when villains do it
Played as comedy; sexual coercion condemned

content.raw: 3 (manga); higher in the anime dub and live action

content.framing: Alcohol and tobacco shown casually; drugs condemned

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person; slavery and rulers who make themselves gods condemned; self-giving love (Ace, Kuma, Oden). A Pauline.org reviewer reads Luffy's rescue of Nami as an image of Christ seeking the lost.
frames.concerns: Leering and harassment played for laughs; constant drinking and smoking without cost; violence as the default answer.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for friends; false gods humbled; mercy (Luffy rarely kills).
frames.concerns: A human made into a "sun god" (Nika); undead treated lightly; fighting as heroic (St. Basil, canon 13). Fan-service art weighs on guarding the senses (nepsis).

frames.aligns: Clear good versus evil; courage; freeing the enslaved; loyalty.
frames.concerns: Heroes drink and smoke without consequence (SBC resolutions urge abstinence); the Nika "god" identity; gender-variant characters shown approvingly (BF&M 2000, Article XVIII). Fan service a strong concern under Philippians 4:8. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles, an evangelical anime site, reads Luffy's freedom as a picture of "freedom through a Savior" ([BTT](https://beneaththetangles.com/2021/05/06/one-piece-stirs-a-call-to-freedom-a-call-to-adventure)). Rebellion against evil rulers is admired.
frames.concerns: Plugged In (live action) warns of "content that lurks below these waves": blood, a man sliced in half, profanity, transgender characters, objectified women ([Plugged In](https://www.pluggedin.com/tv-reviews/one-piece/)).

frames.aligns: Liberation of captives (Luke 4:18 resonance); loyalty; false gods unmasked.
frames.concerns: A human awakened as a "Sun God," Haki as "spiritual energy" (Plugged In), zombies and shadow-theft (Thriller Bark), cursed swords: media as an "open door" makes these weigh heavily; alcohol; sexualized art.

frames.aligns: Total depravity on display: power corrupts every unchecked ruler; common grace in a non-Christian story's hatred of slavery; lesser magistrates resisting tyranny.
frames.concerns: Heroes' drunkenness; outlaws as heroes against the magistrate (WLC Q123-133); lascivious pictures (WLC Q139).

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: the worst villains abuse the sword the state holds; grace-like forgiveness of defeated foes.
frames.concerns: Outlaw heroes against authority (fourth commandment); drinking; LCMS and ELCA families differ on gender-variant characters.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: freeing slaves, fighting racism (Fish-Man Island); characters growing toward goodness.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and tobacco shown as cool (holiness bodies ask members to abstain); heroic violence. UMC and Global Methodist families differ on gender themes.

frames.aligns: Myth and fantasy sit comfortably in the tradition (C.S. Lewis); anti-slavery and anti-tyranny themes; found family.
frames.concerns: Harassment gags; drunkenness. Episcopal and ACNA families differ on gender-variant characters.

frames.aligns: Suspicion of state power; Luffy's refusal to rule the islands he frees; care for the weak.
frames.concerns: Freedom is won by force in every arc, which nonresistance rejects at the level of message; drinking; immodest dress. Many conservative families avoid such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, keeping promises, self-sacrifice; family-like bonds; slavery condemned.
frames.concerns: Admired heroes drink and smoke without cost (Word of Wisdom); harassment played as comedy.
Heroes' drinking and smoking (members abstain); undead and a living afterlife (Brook, Thriller Bark) conflict with the teaching that the dead sleep; a human god. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Hatred of human tyranny that echoes distrust of human governments; mercy; freeing slaves.
frames.concerns: Violence as the hero's way (Psalm 11:5); spiritism in zombies, cursed objects and a "sun god"; heroes defy all government, where Witnesses keep neutrality rather than rebellion; gender-variant characters. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Freedom and good overcoming oppression; love among friends.
frames.concerns: Horror and bodily harm as mental imagery to guard against; drinking and smoking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Social-justice core: slavery, racism, aristocracy, erasure of history; gender-variant characters shown with acceptance (CSM).
frames.concerns: Fan service and harassment as comedy; okama characters sometimes used for laughs.

frames.aligns: An Exodus-like hatred of slavery and of rulers who call themselves gods; memory against erased history (Ohara).
frames.concerns: A man revered as a god; gender-variant characters. Tzniut makes fan service a strong depiction concern; Haredi homes would avoid it. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Exodus themes; dignity of the stranger (fish-men); memory against erasure.
frames.concerns: A man worshipped as a god; leering gags. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam; anti-slavery and anti-racism; gender variance shown with acceptance.
frames.concerns: Objectifying humor. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Justice ('adl) against oppressors; freeing slaves as a virtue (Qur'an 90:13); hospitality and keeping promises.
frames.concerns: Heroes' drinking and smoking without cost (Qur'an 5:90); a man revered as a "sun god" touches on shirk; gender-variant characters shown approvingly. Immodest art and leering (lowering the gaze, 24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Dharma as duty to protect the weak; loyalty to a rightful lord (Wano); a righteous war against tyrants (Gita).
frames.concerns: Intoxicants; ahimsa strained by constant fighting.

frames.aligns: Compassion for suffering beings; letting go of hatred (Hody's revenge rejected); impermanence of power.
frames.concerns: Violence as the main way problems end (first precept); intoxicants (fifth precept); ambition ("King of the Pirates") as a life goal.

frames.aligns: Wano's shrines, festivals and loyalty to ancestors honored; gratitude and harmony.
frames.concerns: Self-proclaimed gods are frauds, though real kami are not mocked. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Defending the oppressed and freeing slaves fits the saint-soldier ideal; equality against hereditary caste (Celestial Dragons).
frames.concerns: Admired heroes smoke constantly (tobacco is one of the four kurahits) and drink; lust played as comedy (Sanji). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Oneness of humanity; elimination of prejudice (fish-men); justice.
frames.concerns: Freedom won through violence, against the commitment to non-violence and obedience to government; drinking; fan service. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Basically good beings freeing others; loyalty; survival across all dynamics.
frames.concerns: Heroes' drinking and smoking; violence. Kuma made into a cyborg and other experiments shown as harm. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Freedom; nature and myth (Nika, Elbaph's Norse gods) treated with respect; no stereotyped witches.
frames.concerns: Violence against "harm none." (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Anti-slavery, anti-racism, anti-aristocracy; gender-variant characters shown kindly (CSM); found family.
frames.concerns: Sexualized female designs and harassment gags; okama as comic relief; Anime Feminist argues Oda answered female critics by sexualizing women more ([Anime Feminist](https://animefeminist.com/choosing-toremain-strong-against-female-criticism-the-vindictive-storytelling-of-oda-eiichiro)).

frames.aligns: Human solidarity and inherited will carry meaning; no god rewards virtue; knowledge defended against censorship (Ohara).
Loyalty, honor, duty, gratitude; strong fathers and mentors; good monarchs honored; courage against tyranny.
frames.concerns: Outlaws as heroes and distrust of all government; gender-identity themes (Ivankov, Yamato) and how adaptations localize them (Bounding Into Comics on "New Trans").

frames.aligns: Rebellion against arbitrary authority; self-proclaimed gods exposed; personal freedom and loyalty to those who earn it.
frames.concerns: Harassment gags against the Eleven Rules on unwanted advances. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of the oppressed; justice; welcome for gender-variant people.
frames.concerns: Objectifying humor. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: When a crewmate is wronged, the crew declares war on whoever holds them (Arlong Park, vol. 9; Enies Lobby, for Robin). Zoro's vows and Sanji's chivalry are honored, while revenge as a cycle is rejected (Hody, vols. 62-65).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Pirate King is "the freest person on the sea"; Luffy will not order his crew to stay and leaves freed islands to rule themselves (Philosophy essay). Authoritarian rule is critiqued in nearly every arc.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Chosen kin (nakama) come first; blood families that exploit are condemned (Vinsmoke, vols. 83-87; Big Mom). Luffy also frees strangers and whole nations, which keeps the position below the top.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hereditary divine right is the central enemy (Celestial Dragons and slavery, ch. 502, 521; Kuma's backstory, vols. 108-109). Loyalty is honored only when freely given (Wano's retainers to Oden).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No real-world religion appears; self-proclaimed gods are exposed as tyrants (Enel; the Celestial Dragons). Late in the story Luffy embodies a liberation myth, the "Sun God Nika" (ch. 1044).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A good life is chasing your own dream; each crewmate joins by choice to chase a dream, and that pursuit is the series' engine. Oppressed peoples' survival is shown seriously, so the position stops short of the top.

folkways.japan: The shonen ideal of friendship, effort and victory, and Wano's samurai loyalty and Edo-period setting (vols. 92-100) reflect Japanese norms; the story's strong anti-aristocratic and anti-authoritarian message is its own, and global readers have taken it up as such.

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Its anti-tyranny stance is stated openly in arc climaxes, while the Marines range from decent officers to fanatics.

personified.ideology: Absolute Justice, order at any price

lenses.label: Might makes right
lenses.stance: Critiqued, though power decides most fights

entry.dominant: Libertarianism (liberty and anti-authoritarianism), Classical virtue ethics (loyalty and courage), Communitarianism (the crew and freed peoples), and a critique of Collectivism/authoritarianism. "Anti-authoritarian" is drawn from Wikipedia's account of the themes. The labels Critical theory, Expressive individualism, Communitarianism, Pragmatism and Confucian ethics are our framing, not any source's.

entry.heading: Attack on Titan (Shingeki no Kyojin)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived freely and for the people you love, but freedom pursued through violence spreads the hatred it means to escape; the story asks the reader to keep looking for understanding even when the world is cruel.

frames.aligns: Evil is shown to bring understanding, not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); self-sacrifice for friends; the dignity of the enemy shown from inside Marley; forgiveness (the Blouse family toward Gabi).
frames.concerns: A "devil" origin myth; no hope beyond death; a suicide attempt (CCC 2280-2283).

frames.aligns: Repentance as a long road (Reiner, Gabi); the burden of killing even in war.
frames.concerns: "Devil" pact imagery may be a concern where evil spirits are taken as real; no transcendent hope. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore itself a serious concern.

frames.aligns: Clear picture of sin passed down and of human evil; sacrifice for others; revenge shown to destroy. Views vary by congregation, since each church is self-governing.
frames.concerns: "Devil" pact as myth; no gospel answer.

frames.aligns: Christian writers draw out sin, sacrifice and overcoming evil with good (Thirst.sg and Christ and Pop Culture titles; not opened). Depicts a mass killer without endorsing him.
frames.concerns: Nihilistic voices (Kenny, Zeke); a hero who becomes a mass killer needs careful reading.

frames.aligns: Longing for freedom and deliverance; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": power from a pact with a "devil" (ch. 122); Paths and a spirit world binding a people.

frames.aligns: Realism about total depravity: no one is innocent, including the heroes. Common grace lets readers value the art and its questions.
frames.concerns: Little answer beyond human effort; a suicide attempt (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Two-kingdoms questions: governments lie and wage war, yet order matters. Law exposes guilt (Reiner, Gabi).
frames.concerns: Little gospel (forgiveness is human, not divine). LCMS and ELCA families may weigh the content differently.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace glimpsed in former enemies changing (Gabi, Reiner); social holiness against ethnic hatred.
frames.concerns: Profanity; no transcendent hope. Holiness churches more cautious about the content than UMC.

frames.aligns: Just-war tradition (Article 37) fits the story's questions; forgiveness of enemies; works judged by how they frame good and evil.
frames.concerns: Suicide attempt; no transcendent hope. Episcopal and ACNA families may differ on the gender questions.

frames.aligns: Violence is not shown as heroic in the end: it is a cycle that corrupts everyone, and the ending sides with Armin's choice to talk rather than kill.
frames.concerns: Most conflicts are still settled by force; children trained as soldiers. Old Order and conservative groups avoid most popular media regardless; MC USA families may read it as an anti-war text.

frames.aligns: Courage, sacrifice and family love; repentance of former enemies.
frames.concerns: Eren's preemptive war; no afterlife hope; a suicide attempt.

frames.aligns: Death shown as final rather than as roaming spirits; the cost of hatred; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: The Paths and a "devil" origin myth. Glorified violence is a concern, though the story does not glorify it in the end.

frames.aligns: Christian neutrality echoed: war and nationalism are shown to destroy everyone; honesty about guilt.
frames.concerns: A "devil" pact myth; the military as the main path for the heroes.

frames.aligns: Understanding ends hatred; fear shown as the root of violence.
frames.concerns: Evil, fear and death shown as overwhelming realities; despair.

frames.aligns: Peace-and-justice reading: a critique of ethnonationalism, propaganda and dehumanization; anti-war ending.
frames.concerns: Critics' concern that Holocaust imagery is used carelessly (New Republic, JTA); a female lead centered on a man.

frames.aligns: Memory of persecution and the cost of dehumanization; respect for life.
frames.concerns: Armbands, internment zones and a "euthanasia" plan echo the Holocaust (ch. 86-88, 114); some see antisemitic tropes (Eldians as a "devil" people whose blood carries power). Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Memory of persecution; self-defense debated; respect for life.
frames.concerns: Split on whether the Eldian story honors or distorts Holocaust memory (JTA); Jewish dignity is a stated family concern.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: critique of ethnonationalism and dehumanization.
frames.concerns: Attention to antisemitism and stereotypes: some Jewish fans quoted by JTA felt the Holocaust reduced to a "trope," while Israeli scholars in the same piece read it as about Japanese militarism.

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; courage; the horror of killing innocents is not hidden; collective guilt rejected.
frames.concerns: A "devil" pact as source of power; spiked wine; a suicide attempt (forbidden). Titan nudity is non-sexual.

frames.aligns: Dharma and righteous war are central questions; karma-like cycles of action and consequence across generations.
frames.concerns: Children as soldiers; Eren's certainty without dharma.

frames.aligns: The cycle of hatred and revenge is the core theme; attachment and fear drive suffering; the ending sides with non-hatred.
frames.concerns: Despair; a suicide attempt; spiked wine (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Harmony with others restored only through sincerity; ancestors' burdens.
frames.concerns: No sacred framing; impurity of death everywhere.

frames.aligns: Courage to defend the oppressed; anger and ego shown to destroy (Eren); equality of all people against ethnic hatred.
The oneness of humanity: ethnonationalism and collective guilt are condemned, and the ending turns to dialogue across peoples.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence; the story offers no spiritual answer.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: do not murder; seek to live with the truth (Armin, Hange).
Norse myth echoes (Ymir, the world tree) used without mockery; "harm none" ideal set against the cycle of revenge.
Critique of ethnonationalism, propaganda and dehumanization; women soldiers as equals; anti-war ending.
frames.concerns: Critics on the left are split on whether the story undercuts its own anti-fascism; the alt-right fandom and Holocaust-imagery debate; Mikasa's arc centered on Eren; Hange's gender left vague.

frames.aligns: Truth-seeking (Armin, Hange), dialogue across enemy lines, this-life meaning (Armin's "small moments" answer to Zeke).
frames.concerns: Nihilist voices; a suicide attempt (safe-messaging concern).

frames.aligns: Courage, duty, sacrifice for homeland and comrades; loyalty; realism about human evil; respect for soldiers.
frames.concerns: Moral ambiguity; heroes who commit atrocities; authority shown as lying.

frames.aligns: Rebellion against lying authority (the monarchy, the wall cult); pursuit of truth; compassion over tribal hatred.
frames.concerns: Eren's absolute freedom is shown as a trap; harm to children.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of the enemy; pluralism and dialogue.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Eren's vow of revenge (ch. 1-2) drives the plot, but the story shows revenge spreading hatred (Gabi kills Sasha, ch. 105) and honors forgiveness (the Blouse family toward Gabi). The ending sides with Armin's dialogue over vengeance (ch. 138-139).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Freedom is the core value: birds and the world beyond the walls; "choose so you won't regret it" (vols. 5-8). Governments that lie are overthrown (Uprising arc, vols. 13-17). Eren's absolute freedom is shown as a trap (ch. 139), which keeps the position below the top.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to comrades is honored (Erwin, ch. 80; Hange, ch. 132), but blood loyalty is critiqued: Grisha uses Zeke, Historia defies her father, and ethnic "our people" thinking becomes the Rumbling. Closing hope rests on a cross-national alliance.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The Survey Corps chain of command (Erwin, Levi) is honored; the walled monarchy and the Church are overthrown (vols. 13-17); Marley's ethnic ranks and armbands are condemned (ch. 86-88).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The wall cult hides the truth (vol. 9, Uprising arc); the royal pacifism vow is shown as harmful; truth-seeking by Armin and Hange is honored. Faith appears as cult and myth (ch. 122), not as a guide the story endorses.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Security and survival dominate a world that is "cruel"; courage, duty and sacrifice are honored (ch. 80, 132). Curiosity (the ocean, vol. 22) and Armin's "small moments" answer to Zeke (ch. 137 area, likely) give self-expression a place.

folkways.japan: The military chain of command, duty and self-sacrifice for the group echo Japanese norms of group loyalty; producer George Wada linked the walls to the closed nature of Japanese society (Creator context). Critics also read the island-against-the-world story against Japan's wartime history, a reading Isayama has rejected.

delivery.evidence: New Republic (Amin) and Berkeley Political Review read a clear warning about fascism; no review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Characters state their positions on freedom, revenge and peace openly, and the story gives each side a hearing before its ending.

personified.ideology: Freedom for his people at any cost
Anti-natalist mercy: end suffering by ending births
A child soldier shaped by state propaganda

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Utilitarianism, Might makes right (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Expressive individualism (critiqued), Nihilism (critiqued).

entry.heading: Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived for others. You protect the weak, honor the dead, keep promises, and pass your will to the next generation. A long or powerful life bought by harming others is worth nothing.

frames.aligns: Evil is shown but never made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); self-giving love; mercy toward the repentant; honor for parents and the dead.
frames.concerns: Kagaya's self-detonation framed as heroic (CCC 2280-2283); Buddhist and Shinto afterlife imagery, judged by framing.

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions (Muzan's craving, Kokushibo's envy); repentance at death (Akaza, ch. 156); care for the dead.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real in the tradition, so "demons" made sympathetic can blur the line; non-Christian afterlife scenes. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore itself a concern.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; sacrifice for others; honoring parents (Ephesians 6:1).
frames.concerns: Buddhist and Shinto spirituality shown as real (John 14:6); heroic framing of Kagaya's choice. Views vary by congregation because each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Redemption themes; Equip.org highlights compassion: "Humanizing is the goal, instead of demonizing," and links it to Romans 2:4. Depicts sin without endorsing it.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian afterlife and spirituality; the story's grace has no source beyond human kindness.

frames.aligns: Clear battle between good and evil; courage and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": literal demons, spirit encounters with the dead, a fire-god ritual dance honored by the hero's family, all shown in a positive or neutral light. Views range widely between churches.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: demons are humans whose sin has grown monstrous. Common grace lets families value good art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent scenes framed as noble (WLC Q136 on self-murder); other religions' afterlife shown as real.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: the Corps bears the sword to protect the weak, like lawful authority. Law and gospel: demons cannot save themselves; mercy comes from outside them.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian spirituality. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Holiness of life and works of mercy; prevenient grace has an echo in demons who remember their humanity at the end.
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent scenes; some fan service. Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) usually more cautious about the content than UMC.

frames.aligns: Just war (Article 37) fits the Corps' fight; good and evil judged by framing, in a strong tradition of fantasy literature (C.S. Lewis).
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent scenes framed as heroic. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on gender, not on this content.

frames.aligns: Humility, compassion for enemies, community care.
frames.concerns: Violence shown as heroic is the central concern, and here it is the heroes' main tool throughout (Matthew 5:39). Conservative groups avoid most popular media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family as central and eternal; reunion with loved ones after death; service and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Heroic framing of self-destruction; fan service. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice, care for family, clear good and evil.
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so spirits of the dead meeting the living (ch. 66, 156, 163, 200) and a rebirth epilogue conflict with teaching on the state of the dead.
Spiritism and spirits of the dead are central motifs (Galatians 5:19-21); fighting as the hero's calling.

frames.aligns: Love and goodness outlast evil; compassion over hatred.
frames.concerns: Evil, death and fear are shown as real and powerful forces, against the teaching that they are not part of God's creation.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the marginalized: demon backstories trace harm to poverty and abuse (ch. 96, 154).
frames.concerns: Traditional gender roles; Nezuko's limited voice; the Rising Sun dispute and Korean historical sensitivities.

frames.aligns: Respect for life and its protection; honoring parents (Exodus 20:12); memory of the dead.
frames.concerns: Self-destruction framed as heroic (suicide traditionally forbidden); a fire-god ritual honored. Tzniut makes the red-light arc and outfits a concern; many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Respect for life; honoring parents; memory of the dead; tikkun olam echoes in protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent sacrifice framed as heroic, treated with compassion today; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Protecting the vulnerable; harm traced to poverty and abuse; memory of the dead.
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent sacrifice framed as heroic; Korean historical sensitivities (Rising Sun earrings, Kanto massacre reading).

frames.aligns: Family loyalty, care for a sister, patience (sabr), fighting only to stop oppression, forgiveness preferred.
frames.concerns: Polytheistic ritual and afterlife imagery treated as real; self-destruction framed as heroic, read against the prohibition of suicide (Qur'an 4:29).

frames.aligns: Dharma may require righteous fighting (Bhagavad Gita); family duty and respect for elders; karma and rebirth (ch. 205).
frames.concerns: Few message conflicts; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the gore.

frames.aligns: Draws on Buddhist ideas: craving (Muzan), compassion for all beings, impermanence, a monk-warrior (Gyomei), rebirth (ch. 205).
frames.concerns: Killing is the plot's solution, against the first precept; demons are destroyed rather than released.

frames.aligns: Kagura dance, sun and purity imagery treated with respect; sincerity (makoto) and gratitude in Tanjiro; oni folklore familiar.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; blood and death are sources of impurity, though shown in a fight against evil.

frames.aligns: Service, sacrifice and unity; noble qualities shown as the real strength.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence: fighting is the heroes' path throughout.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: honor parents, help others, do not murder (demons who murder are condemned).
Respect for folk religion, nature and ancestors; "harm none" echoes in protecting the weak; no stereotyping of witches or pagans.
Empathy for the marginalized; harm traced to poverty and abuse; critique of rule by fear.
frames.concerns: Mostly traditional gender roles; Nezuko's silence and adult-form design (Anime Feminist; The Mary Sue); Mitsuri's uniform gag; polygamy played lightly; Korean historical sensitivities; suicide framed as noble.

frames.aligns: Human bonds and the value of a finite life over endless demon life (Kagaya: human thoughts endure, ch. 137); empathy; afterlife scenes read as fiction.
Duty, honor, sacrifice, respect for elders, lineage, protective masculinity. The Federalist praises its "courage, family, strength, and masculine virtue."
frames.concerns: Little in the message; some religious conservatives raise the demonic imagery.

frames.aligns: Compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2); protection of children.
frames.concerns: The story honors self-sacrifice, deference to a revered leader and duty over the self, while self-preservation is the villain's creed, against Church of Satan individualism.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity even of enemies (Tanjiro's mercy); justice for the exploited (Ume, Gyutaro).
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; traditional gender roles; Korean historical sensitivities.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Duty and samurai-style service are honored, but personal vendetta is not: Tanjiro mourns the demons he kills, and mercy toward Akaza and Gyutaro (ch. 96, 154-156) is part of the story's ethic. Defending family drives the plot more than defending one's name.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Demon Slayer Corps has ranks, supply, doctors and discipline (Pragmatic lens). Duty, training and obeying the Corps are celebrated; Muzan's lawless rule by fear is the counter-example (ch. 52).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is the central value: a brother guarding his sister, the Corps as a family-like body, Rui's forced "fake family" as its opposite. The epilogue honors descendants and lineage (ch. 205).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hashira ranks and deference to Kagaya Ubuyashiki are presented with reverence; his servant leadership and self-sacrifice (ch. 137-138) are shown as heroic. Inherited Breathing styles and passing the will down tie worth to lineage and rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Buddhist and Shinto motifs are sincere: the blind monk Gyomei, the fire-god kagura dance, spirits of the dead meeting the dying (ch. 66, 156, 163, 179, 200), a rebirth-style epilogue (ch. 205). Doma's cult, not faith itself, is exposed.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Life is lived for others: protect the weak, keep promises, accept early death (the "Mark"). Hard training and self-sacrifice (Rengoku, ch. 66) are the highest goods.

folkways.japan: The Taisho-era setting, Confucian filial piety, samurai ideals of service and death, and Shinto and Buddhist imagery are Japanese traditional values the story treats as true; many readers from other cultures will see these as the setting's norms more than a message aimed at them.

delivery.evidence: Tallon (Christian Research Journal): "Humanizing is the goal, instead of demonizing." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about compassion and duty are spoken in Tanjiro's lines and shown through the demons' backstories.

entry.title: Tokyo Ghoul
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In an alternate Tokyo, ghouls who look human but must eat human flesh live in secret. University student Ken Kaneki survives a ghoul attack and is surgically turned into a half-ghoul, then learns to survive among ghouls at the cafe Anteiku while hiding his condition from his human friends. The story follows his struggle to keep his humanity amid conflict with the ghoul-hunting CCG.

entry.heading: Goodnight Punpun
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Takes suffering, guilt and the need for repentance seriously; the mother's deathbed apology; the dignity of a wounded person who keeps living; sin is never made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Asano's relativism; no hope beyond human ties; a planned abortion left unjudged (CCC 2270-2275); a comic "God." Sex outside marriage, sexual abuse and repeated suicide on the page are a heavy depiction concern (CCC 2280-2283, 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: Close to a study of the passions (despair, lust, self-love) and of a soul without spiritual guidance; their cost is never hidden.
frames.concerns: Despair is left without any answer of grace or repentance in the tradition's terms; a comic "God" figure. Watchfulness over the senses (nepsis) makes the sexual imagery and suicide scenes a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Honest about the emptiness of a life without hope; sin's consequences are not hidden.
frames.concerns: No hope in Christ or anything beyond survival; relativism; the abortion storyline. Under Philippians 4:8, the sexual content, abuse, profanity and suicide are a heavy depiction concern. Each congregation is self-governing, so views vary.

frames.aligns: A realistic picture of a fallen world and broken homes; the need for rescue that no human romance can supply. Many in this tradition distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer; relativism; the abortion plan. Explicitness is high even for families who "engage" culture.

frames.aligns: No occult or demonic content; a vivid picture of spiritual emptiness; cults shown as deadly.
frames.concerns: No spiritual answer; a comic "God" summoned by a chant; spiritual deception (the Pegasus group) shown ambiguously. Holiness standards make the sexual content a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has a strong echo: no character is innocent, including the protagonist. Common grace lets adults value serious art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Sin without grace; relativism; abortion. WLC Q139 makes the sexual imagery a heavy depiction concern; suicide as self-murder (WLC Q136), treated pastorally.

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: a person crushed by guilt with no word of forgiveness, shown honestly.
frames.concerns: No gospel offered. Entertainment is judged by conscience; LCMS and WELS families are typically more cautious than ELCA about the explicitness.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace has an echo in the friends who keep reaching for Punpun (Sachi); social holiness in who failed these children.
frames.concerns: No grace named; abortion. Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) are far more cautious than UMC about the sexual content and suicide scenes.

frames.aligns: Moral seriousness about suffering and guilt in the line of serious literary fiction; pastoral approach to suicide; works judged by how they frame good and evil.
frames.concerns: Relativism; abortion; no answer of grace. Episcopal and ACNA families may differ on how much adult literary content they allow.

frames.aligns: Community care as the missing thing; the killing leads only to ruin; no violence shown as heroic.
frames.concerns: A world with no church or community to catch anyone, and no answer beyond private survival. Separation from worldly media makes the explicitness a heavy concern; Old Order groups would avoid it, MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family as the thing that matters most, shown by its absence; repentance and forgiveness (the mother).
frames.concerns: No plan of salvation or hope beyond survival; relativism; abortion. For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the sexual content, profanity and suicide put it outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: The cost of broken homes and unhealthy lives is shown, not admired.
frames.concerns: No hope beyond survival; abortion; a comic "God." Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" make the sexual content and despair a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Immorality and violence are shown as harmful, not admired; cults shown as deadly.
frames.concerns: No hope in God's Kingdom; relativism; abortion. jw.org counsel on entertainment that features immorality and violence makes the explicitness a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Love and friendship (Sachi) are what save Punpun's life.
frames.concerns: Despair, sickness and death are presented as the final reality, against the teaching that they have no place in God's creation. Members guard thought ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392), so dwelling on these depictions is a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Honest treatment of mental illness, abuse and family violence; a male abuse survivor taken seriously; compassion for the broken.
frames.concerns: Women often written as damaged or rescuers; the protagonist's coercion little addressed. Suicide scenes against safe-messaging norms are a depiction concern, Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Respect for this life; the duty to preserve life (pikuach nefesh) underlined by its loss; teshuvah in the mother's apology.
frames.concerns: Relativism; abortion views differ from the story's silence; a comic "God." Tzniut and nivul peh make the sexual content and language a heavy concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Choosing life; teshuvah; the dignity of the wounded.
frames.concerns: Relativism; the abortion storyline is not weighed. Degrading sexual content and vulgar speech are a concern under Jewish values of modesty and dignity.

frames.aligns: Honest about abuse, cruelty and exploitation as harm; compassion for the broken.
frames.concerns: Women as damaged rescuers; the protagonist's coercion. Suicide content is a depiction concern, Significant for younger readers.

frames.concerns: Depression framed through trauma; any push toward psychiatric help would run against the church's stance. No content code for fiction.

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility; harm shown as harm (the Rede); no stereotyped witches or pagans.
frames.concerns: Little hope offered. The Rede ("harm none") underlines the abuse and killing.

frames.aligns: Serious treatment of depression, family violence and a male abuse survivor; no glamorized fan service; critique of cult control.
frames.concerns: Women written as damaged rescuers; the protagonist's sexual coercion little addressed. Suicide shown repeatedly, possibly including a hanging, which safe-messaging guidelines advise against.

frames.aligns: This-life focus; human connection and ordinary work as what keeps a person going; critique of cults and magical thinking.
frames.concerns: Little model of recovery. Cruelty and the suicide scenes are a depiction concern, Significant for minors.

frames.aligns: Shows the cost of broken families and absent fathers; no glamour in the sex or violence; responsibility shown by its failure.
frames.concerns: Relativism; abortion; a protagonist who abandons his responsibilities. Content that degrades the good, the true and the beautiful is a depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Life lived now, with no afterlife; critique of cults and of messianic hope; harm to a minor and unwanted sexual advances, which the Eleven Rules condemn, framed as harm.
frames.concerns: Little self-determination shown; Punpun is mostly passive. Harm to children shown on the page is the depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of the wounded; compassion; honest search for meaning without a given answer.
frames.concerns: Women as damaged rescuers; little community repair. Age-appropriateness makes it adult reading.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No act of revenge or defense of honor is celebrated: Punpun's killing of Mitsuko (ch. ~113-114) leads only to flight and loss, and Asano says he does not think Punpun is a "good person."

Order vs freedom.evidence: No institution rescues anyone, and Asano's frame is pluralist: "the world has many different values, but none of them are 'right.'" The story neither celebrates rules nor romanticizes freedom; the Kagoshima escape fails.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Families are broken (father's assault, Aiko's cult stepmother, Midori's abuse, ch. 50). What helps is a friend who intervenes (Sachi stops Punpun's suicide attempt) and a mother's late apology.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Adult power over children is the main form of power, and it is shown as harmful (Socio-cultural lens). No leader or elder is held up for deference.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion appears as a comic inner "God" voice and as cults that fail to save (Aiko's stepmother; Pegasus's group). The ending rests on ordinary secular survival: a job, time, a few ties.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The ending values plain survival and work, but Sachi's creative ambition and the story's tolerance for many values pull toward self-expression.

folkways.japan: The pressure to appear normal, social withdrawal, silence about family violence and the I-novel tradition of confession are Japanese context the essay notes; the story criticizes these more than it endorses them.

delivery.evidence: Asano (ANN interview, 2018) says the work offers no answers, only questions.
delivery.note: The series avoids stated morals and leaves most of its verdicts open.

personified.ideology: Frank friendship and creative work as a reason to go on
