series.title: Komi Can't Communicate
series.native: 古見さんは、コミュ症です。

entry.heading: Komi Can't Communicate (Tomohito Oda)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a life with others: anyone can be befriended if someone is patient with them, and the effort to reach out, however clumsy, is worth more than looking perfect.

frames.aligns: Dignity of each person (CCC 1700) shown in noticing the silent girl; friendship as self-gift; a chaste romance with honesty toward the rival (ch. 301-305).
frames.concerns: Fan service and lewd gags against modesty (CCC 2521-2524); Najimi's ambiguous gender alongside the Church's teaching on sexual difference; Yamai's obsession played as comedy.

frames.aligns: Humility (Tadano), patient love, community healing a fearful soul.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) against fan-service images; gender as given in Orthodox teaching versus Najimi's play with it.

frames.aligns: Kindness, patience, honesty in a love triangle, no sex outside marriage shown.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test for the fan-service gags and lewd jokes; Najimi's gender presentation read against BF&M Article XVIII; same-sex obsession gags. Each family decides.

frames.aligns: Reaching the lonely and the overlooked (Luke 14:13); not judging by appearances (John 7:24): Komi is not what she seems.
frames.concerns: Fan service; gender ambiguity presented as a running joke; romance and friend-count as the source of meaning.

frames.aligns: Freedom from fear (2 Timothy 1:7 echo in Komi's courage); joyful community. No occult content.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty; traditional teaching on gender; idolizing a person ("Church of Komi" gag).

frames.aligns: Common grace: a well-made, kind story by a non-Christian; idolatry of a person exposed as empty.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 on lascivious pictures applies to the fan-service gags; Najimi read against traditional teaching on male and female.

frames.aligns: Vocation of neighbor-love in ordinary school life; Tadano as the ordinary person who serves.
frames.concerns: Fan service; LCMS and WELS families weigh Najimi's gender ambiguity more than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Social holiness in small acts; welcome of the outsider; "do good" to the anxious and excluded.
frames.concerns: Fan service; holiness churches more cautious than UMC on gender ambiguity.

frames.aligns: Kindness, belonging and honest courtship framed as good; generous reading of comedy.
frames.concerns: Fan service; Episcopal and ACNA families differ on Najimi.

frames.aligns: Humility, community, nonviolence, gentle service to the weak.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media makes a secular anime or manga a concern for Old Order families; fan service; gender play. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Friendship, ministering to the one, chaste courtship, a family that welcomes the boyfriend (with a test).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth on media that is "vulgar" (fan service, lewd jokes); the Family Proclamation's teaching on gender versus Najimi.

frames.aligns: Welcome of the anxious and excluded; mental health treated with empathy; a gender-nonconforming character among friends.
frames.concerns: Critics read Najimi's gender as a punchline (ANN's Faye Hopper) and Yamai as a "psycho lesbian" stereotype; sexualized framing of schoolgirls (CSM).

frames.aligns: Kindness, service, patient friendship, no substances.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed" applied to fan service; traditional teaching on gender; entertainment of "highest quality" (FB 22).

frames.aligns: Kindness, honesty, avoiding violence in the main cast.
frames.concerns: jw.org's question on what God hates: lewd gags and fan service; gender ambiguity and same-sex attraction gags; teen dating not aimed at marriage. No spiritism.

frames.aligns: Love and right thinking overcome fear: Komi's anxiety yields to friendship without medicine.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on fear and embarrassment; lewd gags.

frames.aligns: Kavod habriyot (dignity of each person), hesed, kind speech, guarding against shaming (ona'at devarim).
frames.concerns: Tzniut: mixed-sex school setting, swimsuits and fan service; cross-dressing (Deuteronomy 22:5) and same-sex attraction gags. Many Haredi homes would not have the series.
Fan service; families vary on how the gender gags land.

frames.aligns: Dignity, inclusion, emotional honesty, a gender-nonconforming friend.
frames.concerns: Whether Najimi is respected or mocked; sexualized framing.

frames.aligns: Kindness, patience, mercy and forgiveness; chaste couple; family respect.
frames.concerns: Free mixing and dating; lowering the gaze (24:30-31) for fan service and swimsuits; cross-gender dress and same-sex attraction gags against traditional teaching.

frames.aligns: Seva and patience; friendship (maitri) and kindness to the fearful.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's categories to fan service; views on gender ambiguity vary.

frames.aligns: Compassion for suffering; right speech literally at the center; fear met with patience.
frames.concerns: Attachment and craving (Yamai's obsession) as comedy; third precept read differently across schools.
Kaam (lust) in the fan-service gags and Yamai's obsession; views on gender vary in the diaspora.

frames.aligns: Unity, fellowship, kindness to all, a chaste romance.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life" for lewd gags; teaching on marriage and gender.

frames.aligns: Harmony (wa), sincerity (makoto), gratitude; shrine life shown naturally (Nokoko's family).
frames.concerns: Little to raise; idolizing a classmate as a "goddess" is comic, not a shrine matter.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" in the main cast's kindness; acceptance of difference including gender play.
frames.concerns: Yamai's stalking and kidnapping break "harm none" and are forgiven lightly.

frames.aligns: Communication is a central concept in Scientology's teachings, and the series is about learning to communicate; The Way to Happiness precepts (help others, be worthy of trust, respect others' beliefs); anxiety overcome without psychiatry, which fits the Church's opposition to it.
frames.concerns: Yamai's harm to Tadano forgiven lightly; lewd gags.

frames.aligns: Anxiety and disability shown with empathy; a gender-nonconforming character in the friend group; CBR reads the class-trip scenes as a realistic look at exclusion from gendered spaces.
frames.concerns: Najimi's gender as a punchline (ANN's Faye Hopper: "extremely tasteless"; ANN chat: cross-dressing jokes are "entirely too late"); Yamai as a "psycho lesbian" stereotype; sexualized framing of schoolgirls (CSM: "A teen in a short skirt who is too anxious to speak can be made into a sex object"); anxiety partly a "quirk" (Hopper).

frames.aligns: Human connection as the source of meaning; patience and reason applied to a real condition; no religious framing needed.
frames.concerns: No adult or professional help shown for a clinical condition; quick forgiveness of the kidnapping.

frames.aligns: Patience, manners, loyalty, a chaste courtship, a father who vets his daughter's boyfriend (ch. 317), graduation as a milestone.
frames.concerns: Najimi's gender ambiguity presented to a young audience; lewd and fan-service gags; same-sex obsession gags.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the anxious, the odd and the gender-nonconforming; community as healer.
frames.concerns: Concern about negative LGBTQ portrayals (Yamai; Najimi as gag); sexualized framing.

frames.aligns: Self-expression and refusing labels (Najimi); compassion and empathy (Satanic Temple Tenet 1); loyalty to those who earn it.
frames.concerns: Yamai's stalking and kidnapping break bodily autonomy (Tenet 3); the crowd's herd worship of Komi and quick forgiveness may read as weakness to Church of Satan readers.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Komi's worth is inherent, not won; conflicts end in apologies (Yamai, ch. 26) or honest talk (Manbagi, ch. 301-304), not fights.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Characters work within school rules and group events (trips, festivals, class play); harmony is valued; Najimi's freedom sits inside the system rather than against it.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Friendship across the whole class, 100 friends of every type; family is warm but secondary.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The story pushes from idolizing Komi toward friendship as equals; some school and family deference (father's test, ch. 317).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular daily life with customs kept lightly (shrine family, school rites); no religion guides choices.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Tolerance of quirks and difference, and the quality of relationships, are the core values.

folkways.japan: Reading the air (kuuki wo yomu), group harmony, the shame of standing out, class trips and rooms split by gender, school rites like culture festivals and graduation, and the term komyushō itself are Japanese norms that frame the story more than they form its message. The scenes where Najimi has no gendered group to join (CBR) reflect Japanese school logistics as much as any argument about gender.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Rebecca Silverman calls it "good-natured" with "a distinct lack of cruelty"; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Lessons about friendship and courage are carried by gag-chapter situations and character name puns.

personified.ideology: Ordinary kindness is enough to help

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics.

entry.heading: Kaiju No. 8
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: It is never too late: a good life keeps a childhood promise, does honest work well, and uses whatever power it has to protect others, inside a team that has learned to trust you.

frames.aligns: Dignity of work; perseverance; laying down one's life for others; evil not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Human dignity and the use of a person as a weapon (Kafka's custody); a ghost restoring a heart, judged by framing.

frames.aligns: Struggle to stay human against a monstrous nature; humility; sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) for the gore; spirits of the dead acting in the world.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; hard work; protecting the weak; friendship.
frames.concerns: Spirit and ghost elements late in the story; mild profanity. Each congregation and family decides.

frames.aligns: Second chances, a humble hero, a found-family team; sin (No. 9's predation) depicted, not endorsed.
frames.concerns: Grace in the story has no source beyond human effort and a ghost.

frames.aligns: Clear spiritual-style war between good and evil; courage.
frames.concerns: An oni-styled monster form and spirits of the dead within the hero; may read as an "open door." Views vary by church.

frames.aligns: Common grace in well-crafted art; lawful magistrate bearing the sword; vocation.
frames.concerns: Ghostly intervention in place of providence.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: a lawful defense force protects the people; vocation in ordinary work.
frames.concerns: Little in the message; LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious about gore than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Works of mercy, discipline and steady growth; a hero who keeps his humanity.
frames.concerns: Gore and mild profanity for holiness churches.

frames.aligns: Just defense (Article 37); a strong fantasy tradition that judges by framing.
Humility, service, community trust, mercy to a rival (Hoshina).
frames.concerns: Heroic military force is the central path and the institution is a state army (Matthew 5:39). Conservative groups avoid most popular media.

frames.aligns: Hard work, keeping covenants and promises, service, second chances.
frames.concerns: Mild language and gore; For the Strength of Youth asks whether media invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Dignity of working-class labor; women in leadership; protecting the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Militarism; using a sentient being as a weapon; surveillance of a man who has done no harm.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, service, clear good and evil.
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so Isao's spirit and the warriors' spirits acting (ch. 113, 129) conflict with teaching on the state of the dead.
Violence as the hero's calling (Psalm 11:5); spirits of the dead acting in the world (spiritism); service in a military.

frames.aligns: Goodness and persistence prevail; the hero refuses to be defined by a monstrous body.
frames.concerns: Fear, injury and monstrous matter shown as powerful.

frames.aligns: Protecting life (pikuach nefesh echoes); keeping one's word; honoring a father (Kikoru).
frames.concerns: Spirits of the dead; many Haredi homes restrict secular media altogether; immodest suits and nudity gags (tzniut).

frames.aligns: Protecting life; keeping promises; dignity of work.
frames.concerns: Little in the message; families apply modesty values to the gags.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam echoes in repairing a disaster-struck world; dignity of labor; women leaders.
frames.concerns: The ethics of weaponizing sentient beings.

frames.aligns: Patience (sabr), steady striving, keeping promises (Qur'an 17:34), defending the weak.
frames.concerns: Spirits of the dead acting; oni-style imagery; nudity gags and suits for lowering the gaze (24:30-31).

frames.aligns: Duty (dharma) in one's role, from cleaner to soldier; protecting society; ancestral spirits entrusting a mission.
frames.concerns: Few message conflicts; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to gore.

frames.aligns: Compassion, humility, letting go of regret (ch. 120), the self that is more than its body.
frames.concerns: Killing as the main solution; grudges of the dead living on.

frames.aligns: Kirat karni (honest work), seva, courage to defend others: the saint-soldier ideal.
Work done in service is worship; unity of a diverse team.
frames.concerns: Commitment to non-violence; force is the heroes' path throughout.

frames.aligns: Kami-like disasters, ancestral warrior spirits handing on a duty, a shrine mask, sincerity (makoto).
frames.concerns: Blood and death as impurity, shown in protective combat.

frames.aligns: Respect for ancestors and spirits; "harm none" echoes in protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Using living creatures as weapons and research material.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: be industrious, be competent, fulfill obligations, safeguard others. Struggle is shown without psychiatric framing.
Dignity of working-class labor; women in command; outsiders proving their worth.
frames.concerns: Militarized state, surveillance and detention of Kafka framed as reasonable; sentient beings as weapons; nudity and urination gags.

frames.aligns: Human effort, science and cooperation defeat disaster; the ghost scene read as fiction.
Duty, perseverance, honest work, protective masculinity in an ordinary 32-year-old man, respect for rank and fathers.
Inherent worth of a person labeled a monster; justice for workers.
A man rejects the label authority gives him and proves himself on merit (Church of Satan stress on self-reliance); protection of children (Eleven Rules).
frames.concerns: Self-sacrifice for the group and deference to military rank run against Church of Satan individualism.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is earned by work, not name: Kafka rises from cleaner to platoon leader (ch. 129). Kikoru's burden of the Shinomiya name is eased rather than defended. No vendettas.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Defense Force's rules, ranks and evaluations are trusted; Kafka submits to custody and testing (v4-5) and is allowed his power only within limits (ch. 129).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Civic duty and a found team come first; family (Isao and Kikoru) is a strong secondary thread.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Clear ranks and a Director General with life-and-death say over Kafka (v5); offset by merit-based rise and a 32-year-old outsider's acceptance.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Science, research and engineered weapons drive the plot; the spirit layer comes only at the end (ch. 113, 129).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Chasing a dream is celebrated, but the dream is service and security for others; disaster preparedness is a civic norm.

folkways.japan: The senpai-kohai hierarchy, the workplace-evaluation feel of the Defense Force, disaster drills and shelters (Japan's earthquake culture), the oni design and Edo-era spirits reflect Japanese norms and folklore that the story uses as setting rather than as a message to the reader.

delivery.evidence: That Sounds Awesome praises its "never too late" message; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about persistence is carried mainly by Kafka's situation as a 32-year-old latecomer.

personified.ideology: Persistence; it is never too late
Predation and absorbing others to grow

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Pragmatism, Communitarianism, Transhumanism (explored), Secular humanism.

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: Part 7–Steel Ball Run
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Steel Ball Run
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 スティール・ボール・ラン

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 7: Steel Ball Run
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is the honest pursuit of one's own fulfillment and growth through hardship and friendship: getting from "minus to zero" by one's own effort, not by power taken from others. No nation, and no sacred object, justifies sacrificing the powerless.

frames.aligns: Relics as holy and not to be owned for profit or power (the veneration of relics, CCC 1674); the abuse of the sacred for power is condemned in Valentine; a nun's search for forgiveness; the Saint's call not to shoot. Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7), though Valentine is given dignity.
frames.concerns: Christ's body remains on earth and he dies again (ch. 67), against the Resurrection and Ascension (CCC 645-667); relics shown as magic power sources, which the Catechism would call superstition (CCC 2111); sexual threats against a minor (ch. 60-61).

frames.aligns: Relics are deeply venerated in the tradition, and the story treats the Corpse as holy and powerful; repentance (Hot Pants); the ruler who seizes holy things falls.
frames.concerns: Christ's body divided into weapon-granting pieces and fought over can read as profaning the holy; a fictional Christ who dies again; a cartoon image of Christ outside the icon tradition. Guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs the gore.

frames.aligns: Clear condemnation of a ruler who uses religion for power; personal repentance; friendship and perseverance.
frames.concerns: The bodily Resurrection and Ascension (Acts 1:9-11; Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article II) are changed; relics carry saving power, which many Baptists reject as superstition; violence and language. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Engaging culture: a Christ figure whose word is "do not shoot," a hero who must get from "minus to zero," and a villain who uses God for national power. Depicts without endorsing.
frames.concerns: The story's Christ dies again and his body is a power source, unlike the gospel's empty tomb. Grace is earned or obtained, not given.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; the Holy One's power cannot be seized by the wicked.
frames.concerns: Supernatural power drawn from body parts, spirit appearances (Gyro's ghost, ch. 89) and Christ's power used for killing can read as an "open door" to spiritual confusion.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value the craft; the sovereign God's things cannot be owned; human pride (Valentine) falls.
frames.concerns: Images of Christ are a concern for many under the second commandment (Heidelberg Catechism Q96-98; Westminster Larger Catechism Q109); relic power echoes what the Reformers rejected.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: the earthly ruler who tries to control holy things is judged; vocation and friendship.
frames.concerns: Relic power and a Christ who dies again; graphic violence. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Repentance and growth in character (Johnny, Hot Pants); concern for a condemned child (Marco).
frames.concerns: Relics as sources of power; violence; holiness churches more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Imaginative fiction judged by framing (Lewis's tradition); just war versus a ruler's unjust war (Article 37); repentance.
frames.concerns: A Christ who dies again and a divided body; the violence.

frames.aligns: The Saint's only teaching is not to shoot (ch. 58-59); a state that uses holy things for power is exposed, which echoes Anabaptist suspicion of state religion.
frames.concerns: Gunfights are the heroes' main tool, and Johnny ends the story by shooting the president (ch. 89) (Matthew 5:39). Conservative groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Christ's presence in America has an echo in the Book of Mormon (3 Nephi 11), though the story's version differs; repentance; family reconciliation (Johnny's father).
frames.concerns: A resurrected Christ who later dies again conflicts with teaching on the resurrected body; violence and sexual threats. For the Strength of Youth: does it invite the Spirit?

frames.aligns: Critique of Christian nationalism through Valentine; Native land and Black experience raised (Sandman, Pocoloco); a disabled hero.
frames.concerns: Common Sense Media's concerns about stereotypes and few women; Christ's body turned into a commodity.

frames.aligns: The ruler who misuses the sacred falls; repentance.
frames.concerns: The dead are asleep until the resurrection, so Gyro's spirit (ch. 89), the Saint's appearances and the alternate-world doubles conflict with teaching on the state of the dead; relic power.

frames.aligns: A ruler who uses religion for power is condemned, which echoes Witness political neutrality.
frames.concerns: Jesus died on a stake, not a cross, in Witness teaching, and was raised as a spirit; the story shows a cross and a bodily relic with magic power. Spirits of the dead and constant violence (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Love outlasts hate; Johnny's healing comes from mental and spiritual growth more than from the relic.
frames.concerns: Power lives in matter (a corpse), and disease, death and fear are shown as real and transferable (Love Train).

frames.aligns: A ruler's abuse of power is condemned; repentance (teshuvah) has an echo in Hot Pants and Johnny; protecting a condemned child.
frames.concerns: The story is built around veneration of a Christian messiah's relics, which the tradition does not accept; contact with corpses is a matter of ritual impurity; gore. Many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Critique of a leader who uses religion for power; teshuvah; the dignity of outsiders.
frames.concerns: A Christian relic quest at the center; gore and sexual threats. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Critique of nationalism and of religion as a tool of state power; Native and Black voices; tikkun olam echoes.
frames.concerns: Stereotype concerns (Common Sense Media); violence. No antisemitic tropes reported.

frames.aligns: Isa (Jesus) is a revered prophet, and the figure is drawn with dignity; the tyrant who abuses holy things falls; mercy and restraint.
frames.concerns: Depicting prophets is widely forbidden; the story shows Jesus crucified, which the Qur'an denies (4:157-158); power drawn from a prophet's corpse; violence and sexual threats. The JoJo franchise had a 2008 anime controversy over Qur'anic text in an earlier Part (from general knowledge; to verify; not this Part).

frames.aligns: Righteous struggle (dharma); karma echoes in Johnny's "negative" to "zero"; reverence for a saint's remains.
frames.concerns: Few message conflicts; the gore read as tamasic by some families.

frames.aligns: The division of a holy one's remains into relics echoes the division of the Buddha's relics; craving to possess the sacred (Valentine) leads to ruin; "the detour was the shortest path" (ch. 84).
frames.concerns: Non-harm (first precept) against constant killing; relics used to gain power.

frames.aligns: Defending the weak (Gyro for Marco); a ruler's ego and greed are punished; honest work and courage.
frames.concerns: The Gurus rejected relic worship and superstition, and here relics hold power; violence.

frames.aligns: Christ honored as a Manifestation of God; nationalism that harms others is critiqued, close to Bahá'í teaching on world unity.
frames.concerns: Constant violence; a Christ who dies again; relics as power.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and gratitude; respect for sacred remains and their proper enshrinement (sealed in a church, ch. 90-95).
frames.concerns: Corpses and blood bring kegare (impurity), and the story keeps them at the center; little directly touches kami or shrines.

frames.aligns: Respect for land and Native ways (Sandman's critique); the natural world as powerful (the Devil's Palms).
frames.concerns: "Harm none" set against heavy violence; Native spirituality shown mostly through one character.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts on a just government ("Support a government designed and run for all the people") fit the critique of Valentine; personal responsibility (Johnny).
frames.concerns: "Do not murder" against frequent killing by heroes and villains alike.

frames.aligns: Critique of nationalism and of religion fused with state power; a disabled hero; settler-colonial land theft named (IGN; TV Tropes).
frames.concerns: Common Sense Media: "romanticizes 'manifest destiny,'" stereotypes ("lazy-coded Black character," "superhuman Native American"), "only two female characters," positive messages "a little." Sexual threats against a minor.

frames.aligns: Araki: humanity grows through "strength and spirit, without relying on machines or gods" (Wikipedia). The relics are finally set aside, and Johnny's growth is his own; critique of authority and nationalism; disability shown with agency.
frames.concerns: The supernatural is central, but as fiction, not as a claim; heavy violence.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, honor, keeping one's word (Steven Steel), reconciliation between father and son, reverence toward the Saint.
frames.concerns: Patriotism is carried mainly by the villain, though Araki said Valentine's patriotism and goals were potentially just and his fault is exploiting the powerless (Wikipedia). Gore and language.

frames.aligns: Conscience over authority; inherent worth of the outsider; critique of religion used for power.
The individual against the state; a ruler who claims divine favor for his nation is defeated; personal satisfaction as a goal (Araki); no afterlife reward needed for growth.
frames.concerns: The Saint is drawn reverently and his advice is moral; Church of Satan proportional retaliation versus Satanic Temple compassion (Tenets 1-2) would read Johnny's final shot differently.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Personal honor and the duel are celebrated: Gyro's "Pride and honor cannot exist without consent!" (ch. 21), Ringo's "man's world" (ch. 34-39), Johnny's resolve to settle things himself. Law and courts are not trusted (Valentine's cover-up).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The heroes are free agents against a president who uses national power; the frontier race rewards self-reliance.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty is personal: Gyro for Marco, Johnny for Gyro, Johnny's family wound (ch. 42). The civic loyalty of Valentine's nation-first plan is the villain's.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Valentine's napkin hierarchy (ch. 61) is rejected; racers from every background compete, and Pocoloco wins. Gyro still honors his family rank and trade (ch. 21).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The sacred is real and powerful in the story (the Saint, ch. 58-59), but Araki's stated message is growth without gods, and the relics are sealed away.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Endurance, hardship and survival on the trail come first; Araki's theme of "satisfaction" and the stylish designs lean toward self-expression.

folkways.japan: This is a Japanese artist's imagined America. The duel ethic and the "man's world" echo samurai and Western-film codes alike. Respect for teachers and the burden of a family trade (Gyro) reflect Japanese norms. Treating a Christian holy figure as a powerful relic follows a Japanese pop-culture habit of borrowing Christian imagery without Christian doctrine. A Japanese folk legend places Jesus's grave in Shingo, Aomori, after a journey east (from general knowledge; to verify; no source links Araki to it).

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness. Araki respects Valentine's patriotism and courage (via Wikipedia).
delivery.note: Its themes of growth and the state versus the individual come through the race, and the main villain's patriotism is argued at full strength.

personified.ideology: Nation first, whatever the cost to individuals

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Libertarianism (individual versus state), Christian (explored), with Collectivism/authoritarianism and Utilitarianism critiqued.

entry.heading: Fire Punch (Tatsuki Fujimoto)
entry.label: From summaries

content.framing: Condemned (as abuse) but often used as backdrop

frames.aligns: Self-giving to feed the hungry; human dignity against slavery and trafficking; revenge shown to destroy the avenger; Doma's remorse.
frames.concerns: Religion portrayed only as manipulation; incestuous desire and the look-alike romance; suicide attempts with no hope beyond this life; Togata's identity affirmed against Church teaching on the body (Dignitas Infinita, 2024). Inter Mirifica 7 allows depicting evil to aid understanding, but not making it attractive.

frames.aligns: Evil is real and enslaves; a false savior exposed; endurance of suffering.
frames.concerns: A man worshiped as god (idolatry) is the plot engine, with no true sacred to contrast; incest themes; Togata's transition theme; nepsis makes the imagery itself a serious concern.

frames.aligns: Sin has consequences; slavery and abuse condemned; a false god exposed as false.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence and incest themes throughout; suicide; a world without a true God; trans character affirmed. Soul liberty means families decide; many would avoid it.

frames.aligns: Exposes how people create gods to serve their needs (an idolatry theme some evangelicals discuss); sacrificial love; revenge's cost.
frames.concerns: Graphic sexual abuse of children and adults as backdrop; incest; nihilistic tone; Togata's identity affirmed. Engagers may discuss it with adults; most would not give it to teens.

frames.aligns: False religion and bondage shown as harms; freedom of slaves.
frames.concerns: Little occult or demonic content (the frame's heaviest concern), but a man worshiped as god, sexual immorality and violence are pervasive.

frames.aligns: Total depravity on vivid display; idol-making as the human default (Calvin's "idol factory"); common grace lets some value its honesty.
frames.concerns: WLC Q136 on self-murder (suicide attempts); Q139 on "lascivious... pictures"; incest; no redemption beyond human acts.

frames.aligns: Agni cannot save himself or others; false gods fail; self-giving to feed others echoes vocation.
frames.concerns: Sixth commandment (incest, sexual violence); despair and suicide; LCMS and ELCA families may differ on Togata.

frames.aligns: Social holiness critique of slavery and trafficking; love that sacrifices.
frames.concerns: Holiness emphasis on purity; violence and abuse as spectacle; holiness churches stricter than the UMC, which is more open on Togata.

frames.aligns: Imagination judged by framing: abuse is evil, false gods collapse, revenge destroys.
frames.concerns: The sheer weight of sexual violence and incest; suicide; Episcopal and ACNA families differ on Togata.

frames.aligns: Violence and revenge shown as a cycle that consumes everyone; Doma's turn to pacifism (Wikipedia).
frames.concerns: Violence as the story's engine; sexual content; Old Order groups would avoid it entirely; progressive Mennonites might engage the anti-revenge theme.

frames.aligns: Agency and endurance; sacrifice for others; exposure of false prophets.
frames.concerns: Pervasive sexual violence and incest themes; suicide; Togata's transition theme conflicts with "The Family: A Proclamation" on eternal gender.

frames.aligns: Critique of slavery, trafficking and mob religion; a sympathetic trans character; the vulnerable shown as victims of power.
frames.concerns: Survivors of sexual violence treated as backdrop for Agni's pain (Arthur News); possible misgendering in the English text; suicide safe-messaging.

frames.aligns: Exposure of false worship; care for the enslaved.
frames.concerns: Impure and violent content against Fundamental Belief 22; a man worshiped as god.

frames.aligns: Exposure of false religion as manipulation.
frames.concerns: Violence, sexual immorality and idolatry (worship of a man) run through every volume and are the story's fabric (Psalm 11:5; Galatians 5:19-21).

frames.aligns: Endurance and refusing to be defined by suffering; false beliefs shown to have power only through belief.
frames.concerns: The story dwells on pain, fear and bodily harm without relief, the opposite of guarding thought.

frames.aligns: Avodah zarah (idol worship) exposed as human invention; slavery condemned; Doma's teshuvah-like remorse.
frames.concerns: Arayot (forbidden relations, incl. sibling incest) as a theme; sexual violence; suicide. Tzniut and nivul peh make the depiction a serious concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Critique of idolatry and tyranny; the dignity of the enslaved; choosing life ("Live on" echoes Deuteronomy 30:19, our framing).
frames.concerns: Incest themes; sexual violence; the CJLS has supported trans inclusion (2016), so Togata is less of a concern than the abuse content.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam against slavery; a sympathetic trans character; critique of mob religion; no antisemitic content found.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence as backdrop; suicide; suitability is a parental decision under informed autonomy.

frames.aligns: Shirk (worshiping a created being) exposed as false; mercy to orphans and slaves; revenge's cost.
frames.concerns: Incest (Qur'an 4:23) and sexual violence themes; suicide; Togata's transition theme conflicts with most scholarly views; lowering the gaze (24:30-31) makes the nudity a serious concern.

frames.aligns: Duty and endurance; the cosmic time skip echoes cyclical time (yugas), our framing; a karmic loop for Agni and Judah.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content dominates (Gita 17); incest; no sacred treated with reverence.

frames.aligns: Suffering, craving for revenge, and attachment to a lost sister drive the story; impermanence on a cosmic scale; the epilogue's meeting without memory reads like rebirth (our framing).
frames.concerns: Killing (first precept) and sexual misconduct (third precept) are constant; despair rather than release.

frames.aligns: Seva (service) in feeding others; condemnation of oppression.
frames.concerns: Kaam (lust) and krodh (anger) dominate; revenge is the plot's motor, though shown as ruin; a man worshiped as god.

frames.aligns: Unity against slavery; critique of false religion and fanaticism.
frames.concerns: Shoghi Effendi's warning against degrading art and entertainment applies strongly to the sexual violence and its framing.

frames.aligns: Sincerity in Agni's grief; a frozen world thawing could be read as renewal.
frames.concerns: Blood, death and impurity (kegare) everywhere with no purification; a living person made into a god by a crowd rather than through ritual and gratitude.

frames.aligns: Respect for bodily autonomy (Togata); a World Tree image; a world reborn.
frames.concerns: "Harm none" against pervasive harm; sexual violence as backdrop. The Ice Witch is a fabricated villain, not a portrayal of witches as practitioners.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts against murder and for honesty; critique of lies used to control people.
frames.concerns: Constant killing; "do not harm a person of good will"; Agni's pain and despair; the Church's views on mental health care could frame the "mental illness" reading differently.

frames.aligns: Critique of slavery, trafficking and cults; a trans man drawn sympathetically (Horror Press; TV Tropes).
frames.concerns: Women and children used as symbols of Agni's pain rather than as people (Arthur News); sexual violence used for shock; possible misgendering in the English text (Does the Dog Die); suicide safe-messaging.

frames.aligns: Gods as human inventions; meaning made by choice in a world without design; critique of fanaticism and mob rule; free inquiry.
frames.concerns: Cruelty and exploitation shown at length; a bleak view of human nature.

frames.aligns: Warnings about cults, mob rule and revenge; loyalty to family; self-sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Incest themes; sexual violence; nihilistic tone; religion treated only as a lie; Togata's identity affirmed.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of the enslaved and of Togata; the free search for truth against imposed belief.
frames.concerns: Sexual violence as spectacle; suicide; survivors' agency (Arthur News).

frames.aligns: Religion exposed as a tool of control; bodily autonomy (Togata); skepticism toward saviors.
frames.concerns: Harm to children (trafficking, abuse) is central, though committed by villains and condemned; Eleven Rules and Satanic Temple tenets reject it.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge is the premise, but killing Doma brings only more death and a suicide attempt (likely vol. 5); the story does not celebrate personal vengeance.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Ordered powers (Behemdorg, the cult, Sulya's plan) are all oppressive; freed slaves and personal choice are the good.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The sibling bond (ch. 1) and found family (Togata as older sibling; Judah as "Luna") carry the warmth; Agni also feeds strangers.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Slavery and rank are condemned; leaders and gods are exposed.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion and myth are human inventions (Ice Witch, Agni's cult); film, not faith, is Togata's guide.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: A survival world of hunger and cold; Togata's identity and film dream pull toward self-expression.

folkways.japan: The sibling-duty theme and the endurance of pain (gaman) reflect familiar Japanese story values; the cinema obsession reflects Fujimoto's own love of film (noted by Pixiv Encyclopedia and TV Tropes), not a cultural norm.

delivery.evidence: Fandom Post says it "acts meaningful"; Indiecator calls the later story "a pseudo-philosophical mess". Neither calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about belief, fiction and pain come through ambiguous events rather than stated morals.

personified.ideology: Enduring pain and playing the role others need
Sacrificing a few lives to save a world
Faith in a savior turned to zeal

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (explored), Postmodernism (belief and fiction), Might makes right (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued).

series.title: Tokyo Ghoul:re
series.native: 東京喰種-トーキョーグール-:re

entry.heading: Tokyo Ghoul:re
entry.label: From summaries

content.framing: Shown within love (Kaneki and Touka); predatory desire shown as menacing

frames.aligns: Dignity of the enemy; forgiveness and reconciliation; corrupt power judged; marriage and openness to a child at the end (ch. 179). Evil is shown as evil, not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Sex before marriage on the page (ch. 125); Arima's suicide framed as noble (CCC 2280-2283); gore and nudity that "Ethics in Communications" warns against.

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions; repentance-like turn in Kaneki; love of enemies.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs heavily against ch. 125 and the gore; Eto's mock "new god" (ch. 43) and the cross-shaped kagune of an abuser (ch. 169, 172) touch reverence for holy things.

frames.aligns: Sin has consequences; marriage and fatherhood as responsibility; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Phil 4:8 test: explicit sex outside marriage, gore, an honored suicide; salvation is self-made. Each congregation and family decides (soul liberty).

frames.aligns: A redemption arc, enemy-love and reconciliation; Christian readers (Beneath the Tangles) engage it as a story of identity and "tragic hope."
frames.concerns: Ch. 125 and the gore; no Christ-figure redemption. Families split between "engage" and "separate."

frames.aligns: Clear battle between destructive and protective power; deliverance-like rescue of Kaneki from Dragon (ch. 160-163).
frames.concerns: Possession-like inner voices (ch. 53, 75, 158-159), Eto's "god" claim, sexual content; media as an "open door."

frames.aligns: Total depravity on every side; corrupt magistrates fall; common grace allows valuing a serious work.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 lists "lascivious... pictures"; ch. 125 is a direct concern. No providence shown.

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: people cannot save themselves; vocation (Urie, Ui) inside a broken institution.
frames.concerns: Sexual content and gore; confessional (LCMS, WELS) families stricter than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: care for the hunted and the orphaned (Goat's children, ch. 131); reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule on diversions makes the sex chapter and gore heavy for holiness churches; less so for many UMC families.

frames.aligns: Judged by how good and evil are framed: cruelty condemned, mercy rewarded, marriage at the end.
frames.concerns: Premarital sex on the page and the honored suicide; ACNA families stricter than Episcopal ones.

frames.aligns: The cycle of violence is broken by forgiveness and a negotiated peace; the CCG is replaced.
frames.concerns: Violence remains the main means of change and is often heroic; Old Order groups avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Agency, repentance, marriage and family as the end of the story.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; ch. 125 (sex outside marriage, nudity) and gore are the issue.

frames.aligns: Critique of state violence, purges and child soldiers; inclusion of a trans character; reconciliation.
frames.concerns: The trans character's arc is sexualized and pathologized (No Flying No Tights); fan glamour of violence.

frames.aligns: Consequences of evil; care for the vulnerable; family at the end.
frames.concerns: Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed": horror, gore and a sex chapter weigh heavily.

frames.aligns: Prejudice shown as wrong; peace preferred.
frames.concerns: Violence is constant and settles the conflict (Psalm 11:5); sexual immorality on the page (Galatians 5:19-21); spiritistic inner voices.

frames.aligns: Hope, healing and reconciliation at the end.
frames.concerns: "Stand porter at the door of thought": bodily horror, disease (the ROS ghoul-making illness, ch. 164-165) and death dominate.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh and the value of each life; warning against dehumanizing a people; marriage and a child.
frames.concerns: Tzniut and nivul peh make the nudity, sex and language serious; cannibalism; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Respect for life; repair after catastrophe (the joint agency, ch. 179); forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Dignity of speech and modesty weighed against ch. 125 and gore.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: a broken society rebuilt; minority rights; informed autonomy.
frames.concerns: Watch for stereotypes: the cannibal clan "from the Middle East" (ch. 149); the trans character's treatment.

frames.aligns: Justice against oppression (Furuta's purge); mercy; patience under suffering.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) and the sex chapter; human flesh as the deepest taboo (49:12 image); an honored suicide; the cannibal clan's "Middle East" origin (ch. 149) may read as a stereotype.

frames.aligns: Karma of violence returning on all; dharma in impossible duties; householder life at the end.
frames.concerns: Ahimsa traditions find the premise repellent; tamasic content (Gita 17).

frames.aligns: Craving as the root of suffering; "the world merely exists" (Ishida) echoes non-attachment; compassion for enemies.
frames.concerns: First precept broken constantly; entertainment avoided on observance days.

frames.aligns: Sant-sipahi: fighting to protect the oppressed; equality of all people.
frames.concerns: The five vices (lust, anger) shown in excess; intoxicant and meat taboos make the premise jarring.

frames.aligns: The oneness of humanity realized as coexistence; unity in diversity.
frames.concerns: A "chaste and holy life" weighs against ch. 125 and degrading content.
Blood, corpses and death as kegare on almost every page; no shrines mocked.

frames.aligns: Balance restored between two kinds of beings; respect for the unlike.
A being's identity surviving memory loss and implanted overlays (Haise's recovery, ch. 53); The Way to Happiness precepts on not murdering and honoring others.
frames.concerns: Medicalized control (Quinx surgery, Rc suppressants) and the psychiatric framing of trauma conflict with the Church's opposition to psychiatry; violence. No Scientology guidance on manga found.

frames.aligns: Critique of state purges, fear-driven policy and child soldiers; minority coexistence achieved; a trans character in a major role.
frames.concerns: No Flying No Tights: the trans reveal is "trans body horror," Mutsuki lacks "real agency," and it did not recommend the book for libraries; safe-messaging concerns about the honored suicide.

frames.aligns: Meaning made by human choice in an indifferent world ("the world merely exists"); reason and science cure the ROS crisis (ch. 179); free inquiry.
frames.concerns: Pseudoscience-like biology is fiction, not fact; violence glamorized by fans.

frames.aligns: Marriage and family as the happy ending; duty and loyalty; corrupt elites removed.
frames.concerns: Sex before marriage, gore and language; heavy anti-authority strand; gender identity theme.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity extended to the "other"; justice; a free search for meaning.
frames.concerns: Stereotype concerns (Mutsuki; the "Middle East" clan) and violence.

frames.aligns: The Satanic Temple's tenets of compassion and justice and the Church of Satan's self-determination fit the rebellion against a corrupt order and Kaneki's self-chosen path.
frames.concerns: Non-consensual harm (Mutsuki's captivity, Torso) conflicts with TST's bodily autonomy tenet and the Eleven Rules on harming children (the Oggai, Donato's orphans).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge cycles are broken by forgiveness (Mutsuki forgiven, ch. 179; Goat and CCG ally, ch. 150). Duels of honor still recur (Kaneki and Arima, ch. 74-83; Uta and Yomo's "fun" fight, ch. 169-171).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The secret Washuu order and Furuta's purge are condemned (ch. 83, 127), but the ending builds a new shared institution (Tokyo Security Committee, ch. 179) rather than freedom from rule.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Marriage, a child and family gatherings close the story (ch. 131-132, 179), while the alliance widens loyalty to former enemies (ch. 150).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A hidden aristocratic clan breeding a "pure bloodline" is the villain (ch. 101); investigators who question rank are honored (Urie, ch. 133).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Christian imagery is symbolic (ch. 31.5, 43, 159); science and research cure the ROS crisis and half-human lifespans (ch. 179).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival dominates the war, but the end values tolerance, choosing one's own identity (Haise and Kaneki merging, ch. 53) and quality of life.

folkways.japan: The workplace-family feel of the Quinx household and the senpai-kohai bond of Haise and Arima reflect Japanese organizational norms; Urie's struggle between obeying orders and conscience (ch. 132-133) and the wedding-and-family ending follow familiar Japanese story patterns. These are context, not the story's own argument.

delivery.evidence: Beneath the Tangles finds its dark themes "authentic"; No Flying No Tights criticizes Mutsuki's handling; neither calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Coexistence and the choice to live are argued through Kaneki's confrontation with Furuta's nihilism.

personified.ideology: Accept past sins and choose to live
Serve a cause in secret and pass it on
Hidden aristocracy ruling through the CCG

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Absurdism, Critical theory, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Communitarianism, Nihilism (critiqued).

entry.heading: Haikyu!!
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Find what you love and give it everything, but you cannot fly alone: each person's strengths, and weaknesses, matter only inside a team. Losing is part of the game and a reason to grow, not the end of your worth.

content.frequency: Pervasive outside the book; rare inside

frames.aligns: Teamwork as a common good; each player's gifts serve the whole (1 Corinthians 12, "many parts, one body"); forgiveness and restoration (Ennoshita); the dignity of the small and overlooked; mentors who protect a player's health (ch. 365). Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7): arrogance and violence are outgrown or stopped.
frames.concerns: Some swearing, including God's name in vain once (Plugged In, film); comic ogling of Shimizu. Sport can become an all-consuming good.

frames.aligns: Humility learned through defeat; discipline and struggle (podvig) as the road to growth; the "King" who must learn to serve others (Kageyama).
frames.concerns: Watchfulness (nepsis) asks what a constant diet of competitive excitement forms; mild profanity.

frames.aligns: Philippians 2:3-4 ("in humility value others above yourselves") fits the team ethic; hard work and perseverance; repentance and reconciliation after the fight (ch. 82).
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test on language ("damn," occasional stronger words in subtitles); a smoking coach and adult drinking. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Colossians 3:23 ("work at it with all your heart"); encouragement after mistakes (Common Sense Media notes Hinata lifts teammates instead of tearing them down). The Beneath the Tangles blog reads Ennoshita's restoration as grace, comparing Peter (John 21).
frames.concerns: No faith content; mild language. Many evangelicals would treat this as "engaging culture" with little to redeem.

frames.aligns: Boldness, enthusiasm, perseverance; no occult practice.
frames.concerns: Folk words such as "guardian deity," "Demon Crow" and oni (Plugged In notes "guardian deity" and oni in the film) are figures of speech, but some families who see media as an "open door" may note them.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a well-made story by a non-Christian that tells the truth about effort, limits and community. Vocation: each position has its calling.
frames.concerns: Sport can become an idol; no reference to God's glory as the chief end (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q1).

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora; vocation; worth not destroyed by failure: losses are "chances to grow" (Common Sense Media).
frames.concerns: Grace alone versus a world where effort earns everything; LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious than ELCA families about language.

frames.aligns: Growth toward maturity through discipline and community; mutual accountability (a "class meeting" spirit in the team).
frames.concerns: Wesley's test of diversions "used in the name of the Lord Jesus"; holiness churches would weigh language and the smoking coach; the United Methodist Church is much more open.

frames.aligns: A story that frames good and evil clearly at human scale: pride outgrown, cheating absent, effort honored.
Yieldedness to the community (Gelassenheit): no player wins alone; humility; peaceful resolution of the fight.
frames.concerns: Old Order groups avoid such media; competition and national glory (Olympics, ch. 402) sit uneasily with separation from the world and nonresistance. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Hard work, self-improvement, setting goals, service to others, respect for leaders; healthy living ("Food Becomes Muscle," ch. 369). For the Strength of Youth asks for entertainment that invites the Spirit, and this largely fits.
frames.concerns: Some profanity; a smoking coach and adult drinking (the Word of Wisdom).

frames.aligns: Inclusion of the overlooked (the short player, the quitter, the substitute); justice as fair play; mentors who protect the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Women mainly as managers; an all-male core (critics in High Yellow and SYFY).

frames.aligns: Health and wholeness: rest, diet and medical sense (ch. 365, 369); discipline; no substances among the players.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": the excitement of competition is the series' fuel; Ellen White's writings warn against amusements that stir competitive passions (from general knowledge; to verify). A smoking coach; mild profanity.

frames.aligns: Cooperation, honesty, avoidance of violence (the fight is stopped), no occult practice, respect for elders.
frames.concerns: Witness publications counsel against a competitive spirit (Galatians 5:26) and against nationalism; the Olympic finale celebrates national teams (from general knowledge; to verify). Mild profanity; the coach's smoking.

frames.aligns: "Stand porter at the door of thought": the series is free of fear-inducing imagery; confidence and right thinking help players overcome fear (Asahi, Yamaguchi).
frames.concerns: Takeda's lesson in ch. 365 points to medical care and "rationality" when Hinata is ill, a different approach to healing from the church's prayer-based practice; members decide this for themselves.

frames.aligns: Effort (hishtadlut); honest self-assessment (cheshbon hanefesh); humility (anavah); respect for teachers; Pirkei Avot 4:1 ("Who is honored? One who honors others") fits the respect for opponents.
frames.concerns: Many Haredi homes restrict secular media; Modern Orthodox families are selective. Crude speech (nivul peh) in English versions; comic ogling (tzniut).

frames.aligns: Community, effort, mentorship, kind speech mostly kept; repair after the fight.
Informed autonomy; each person's dignity; inclusion of the overlooked; tikkun olam on a small scale (a team that lifts its weakest).
frames.concerns: Little to raise; women's roles are limited.

frames.aligns: Striving for excellence (ihsan); patience (sabr) in defeat; brotherhood; humility against arrogance (kibr); respect for teachers.
frames.concerns: Profanity in English versions; adults drinking and smoking; comic ogling and locker-room shirtlessness (lowering the gaze, 24:30-31). Scholars differ on images of living beings and on entertainment generally.

frames.aligns: Svadharma: each player finds his own role (setter, decoy, libero); disciplined action; the Gita's call to act without being crushed by results (2:47) echoes the dignity of losing.
frames.concerns: Rajasic passion and desire to win run high; mild language.

frames.aligns: Right effort and concentration; impermanence (each tournament ends, "Our Spring Comes to an End," ch. 367); compassion among teammates; loss accepted.
frames.concerns: The story is driven by craving to win ("Hunger," ch. 219 and ch. 396 by title); ego is softened but not let go. Lay Buddhists on observance days avoid entertainment.

frames.aligns: Seva (service): players serve the team; humility over haumai (ego), shown in Kageyama's change from "King"; chardi kala (rising spirit) after defeat.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; anger and pride appear but are outgrown.

frames.aligns: Unity and cooperation as the source of strength; excellence as service; respect across nations (Hinata in Brazil, Oikawa in Argentina).
frames.concerns: Competition is the frame; the call to a "chaste and holy life" would note mild language and drinking.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) of effort; gratitude to seniors and mentors; harmony (wa) within the team; crows and foxes as familiar symbols. No disrespect to shrines or kami.
Personal growth, self-knowledge, community; "harm none" largely kept (the fight is stopped, health is protected).
frames.concerns: No portrayal of witches or pagans; nature has little role.

frames.aligns: "Be competent" (The Way to Happiness); balance of the dynamics: self, family, group (the team) and humankind (international play); no psychiatry content. The church's own materials say little about anime.
Inclusion of an undersized player; emotional openness among boys; mentors who put health first (ch. 365); respect across countries; a sport that drew many girls and women as fans (AFP; SYFY).
frames.concerns: Women mostly in support roles; comic ogling of Shimizu; critics call the managers "cheerleaders" (High Yellow comment).

frames.aligns: Human effort, reason and analysis win; failure as feedback; dignity and respect for every player; no supernatural claims.

Discipline, duty to the team and school, respect for elders and seniors, meritocracy, gratitude, perseverance, national pride (Olympics, ch. 402); traditional marriage in the epilogue (Tanaka and Shimizu).
Inherent worth of each person, including the short and the substitute; interdependent web (no one wins alone); free search for one's path after high school.

Self-development and competence; each person choosing his own path (Hinata leaves for Brazil, "Freedom," ch. 386); no false piety; respect earned by results. The Satanic Temple's tenets on compassion and correcting mistakes fit the team ethic.
frames.concerns: The Church of Satan's individualism sits uneasily with a story that subordinates the self to the group; humility is praised as a virtue. (Range: TST closer to A; Church of Satan closer to C.)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Rivalries are settled on the court under the rules; respect for opponents is constant (Plugged In: teams compliment each other's plays). The fight (ch. 82) and Oikawa's near-blow (Inter-High flashback) are stopped by teammates. Pride matters, but insults are not answered with force.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Team discipline, set roles and training camps; coaches' rules protect players (ch. 365). After the skip, the story celebrates each player's free choice of path (Hinata to Brazil, "Freedom," ch. 386).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty goes to team and school, and to rivals across schools, not to family or clan. Families appear mostly in backstory (ch. 88, 387).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senpai-kohai respect, captains and coaches deferred to; but places on the court are earned, first-years start, and Kageyama's "King" tyranny (ch. 5-6) is rejected.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith shapes choices; analysis, data, diet and medical sense win (ch. 365, 369). School club traditions and Karasuno's legacy keep it from the far end.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard work, discipline and endurance are central; so are joy in play, personal style and choosing one's own life after school.

folkways.japan: The senpai-kohai hierarchy, the club-activity system, bowing to opponents, team managers, and the emotional weight of the third-years' last tournament are Japanese school norms, shown as setting rather than argued for. The story's own message (cooperation, effort, respect) leans more civic and less hierarchical than the Confucian cluster's placement.

delivery.evidence: ScreenWise: "inspiring without being preachy."
delivery.note: Lessons about teamwork and effort come through matches, and rival teams' views are treated with respect.

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Pragmatism, Confucian ethics; Nihilism ("it's just a club") and Might makes right critiqued.

series.title: My Dress-Up Darling
series.romaji: Sono Bisque Doll wa Koi wo Suru
series.native: その着せ替え人形は恋をする

entry.heading: My Dress-Up Darling (Shinichi Fukuda)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from loving what you love without shame, doing your craft with care, and being accepted by someone who admires the real you; mockery of a person's passions is the wrong to be undone.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance; Marin's open enjoyment of erotic media); Neutral (fan service gags)

frames.aligns: Work and craft as dignified (Gojo's vocation); respect for a grandparent; Gojo's chastity of the eyes; the romance ends in marriage and a child.
frames.concerns: Inter Mirifica 7: evil not made attractive; here a minor's enjoyment of pornographic games is affirmed and fan service of teens is the art's habit (CCC 2354 on pornography; 2521-2524 on modesty).

frames.aligns: Humility and patient craft; love that serves (Gojo's sewing); family continuity.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the framing of teen bodies a heavy concern; a monastic habit used as a costume and an eroge "Saint" setting treat holy dress lightly.

frames.aligns: Kindness, diligence, encouragement of the outsider; marriage as the end of the romance.
frames.concerns: Philippians 4:8 test fails on many pages (CSM: "a lot" of sex and nudity); adult games normalized; 1 Timothy 2:9 on modest dress, cited by a Christian critic (Holy Anime Wars). Families decide under soul liberty.

frames.aligns: "Don't be ashamed" of a God-given gift; Gojo's respect and self-control; the outsider welcomed.
frames.concerns: Depicting versus endorsing: the story endorses Marin's eroge fandom and plays a love-hotel shoot for laughs; framing sexualizes teens. Engage-or-separate views differ by family.

frames.aligns: Joy, encouragement, restoration of a wounded boy's confidence.
frames.concerns: Holiness standards on modesty and separation from worldliness; media as an "open door" to lust. No occult content.

frames.aligns: Common grace in craftsmanship and the real research behind the cosplay; vocation of the doll maker.
frames.concerns: WLC Q139 names "lascivious... books, pictures" among sins against the seventh commandment; the fan service is the test case.

frames.aligns: Vocation and daily work; honoring an elder (Fourth Commandment); marriage at the end.
frames.concerns: Sixth Commandment: "lead a sexually pure and decent life" in word and deed; framing of teens and adult games. LCMS and WELS families more cautious than ELCA.

frames.aligns: Diligence, kindness, small community of support.
frames.concerns: Wesley's rule to avoid books that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; holiness churches would avoid it; UMC families vary.

frames.aligns: A story judged by its framing: craft, acceptance and gentle romance leading to marriage.
frames.concerns: Fan service of minors and the love-hotel comedy; Episcopal and ACNA families weigh these differently.

frames.aligns: Humble craft, a quiet young man, care for an elder.
frames.concerns: Separation from worldly media; plain dress ideals make costume display and partial nudity a strong concern. MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family, eventual marriage and a child; developing talents (parable of the talents); kindness.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: entertainment that does not invite the Spirit; modesty and the law of chastity in thought; pornographic games affirmed.

frames.aligns: Challenge to gendered hobbies; welcome for crossplay and queer-coded characters; outsider affirmed.
frames.concerns: Sexualization of minors; body-image pressure on a teen model left unexamined (A.V. Club).
Fundamental Belief 22 on entertainment "of the highest quality"; "by beholding we become changed" weighs heavily on fan service; adornment and display.
jw.org counsel to avoid what features immorality; pornographic games and sexualized display treated positively; a nun's habit as costume.

frames.aligns: Fear and shame overcome by love and acceptance; healing of thought in Gojo.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on sensual images is a mental influence to guard against; body-anxiety and diet thinking.

frames.aligns: Craft and diligence; kibbud zekenim (honoring the grandfather); marriage and a child as the end.
frames.concerns: Tzniut: mixed-sex teen intimacy, partial nudity and display throughout; many families would not have it in the home.

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person's interests; family; marriage.
frames.concerns: Modesty and the sexualization of teens; families apply values case by case.

frames.aligns: Inclusion, gender-nonconforming hobbies affirmed, emotional honesty.
frames.concerns: Sexualization of minors and diet pressure; informed autonomy leaves it to families.

frames.aligns: Diligence, kindness, honoring an elder, marriage as the outcome.
frames.concerns: Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) and modest dress: the series is built on display; unchaperoned teen intimacy; pornographic games affirmed; images of the body.

frames.aligns: Craft as dharma passed in a family line (the doll workshop); seva in sewing for friends.
frames.concerns: Some families apply the Gita's tamasic and rajasic categories to sensual media; brahmacharya for students.

frames.aligns: Right livelihood in craft; compassion for the shamed boy; non-judgment of others' joys.
frames.concerns: Craving and attachment to appearance (diet arc, fame); sensual imagery as a feed for the mind.
Kaam (lust) among the five vices is often played for laughs; ego and attachment to appearance.

frames.aligns: Work as worship (craft), service, unity, marriage.
frames.concerns: The call to a "chaste and holy life" and against degrading entertainment conflicts with the fan service.

frames.aligns: Craft lineage, sincerity (makoto), the Hinamatsuri doll tradition shown with care and real research (Iwatsuki workshops).
frames.concerns: Little doctrinal concern; some may find the doll tradition's sacred roots treated only as trade.

frames.aligns: Self-expression, body confidence, gender freedom, "harm none" in mutual respect.
frames.concerns: Diet pressure and teen sexualization run against harm none for some families.

frames.aligns: Competence and work ethic; communication solves problems; respect for others' choices.
frames.concerns: The Way to Happiness precepts on decency and setting a good example; sexualized teen art.

frames.aligns: Challenge to gendered hobbies; crossplay and queer-coded characters treated kindly; a confident heroine (Bleeding Cool: "nothing wrong with being confident and comfortable with your body").
frames.concerns: Sexualization of minors and the camera's male gaze (Anime Feminist); Juju's nonconsensual exposure gag (ANN); unchallenged diet culture (A.V. Club).

frames.aligns: Meaning from craft, friendship and love; no supernatural framing; free expression.
frames.concerns: Critical thinking about how media sexualizes teens and promotes dieting.

frames.aligns: Respect for a grandparent and an inherited craft; marriage, children and a family business at the end; a gentlemanly hero.
frames.concerns: The good, the true and the beautiful versus sexualized display; adult games normalized for teens; the love-hotel comedy.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of the mocked boy; acceptance of crossplay and difference; free search for meaning in a hobby.
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness and how girls' bodies are portrayed.

frames.aligns: Indulgence without shame (Church of Satan); self-expression against conformity; bodily autonomy (Satanic Temple Tenet 3) in Marin's confidence.
frames.concerns: Concern for children in the Eleven Rules may apply to teen sexualization; Juju's coercion of Gojo.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Worth is inherent: Gojo's value is in his craft, not reputation; mockery is answered by acceptance, not retaliation (ch. 1). Juju's grudge ends in apology (fan wiki).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Individuals choose their hobbies, dress and display; school and parents rarely set limits; Marin lives largely on her own (to verify).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Gojo's grandfather and family craft matter, but the chosen cosplay community is the main circle of care.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Peers are equals across popularity lines (gyaru and loner); respect for the grandfather and for skilled senior cosplayers (Amane, Akira).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secular daily life; a traditional craft honored but valued as art and trade, not religion.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-expression and tolerance are the central values: cosplay, crossplay, "love what you love." The diet and modeling arcs show some appearance pressure.

folkways.japan: The hina doll craft and Hinamatsuri, apprenticeship within a family workshop, the gyaru and otaku subcultures, love hotels as a known institution, and the school-uniform setting are Japanese norms that frame the story rather than form its message. The seinen-magazine convention of fan service with high school characters is also a Japanese publishing norm, debated within and outside Japan.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Rebecca Silverman sums it up as "not being ashamed of what you love"; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its acceptance message is carried by the leads' relationship and cosplay arcs, alongside fan service that critics discuss.

personified.ideology: Unashamed enthusiasm for what one loves

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics (craft), Communitarianism (fandom), Hedonism.

entry.title: Death Note
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: Light Yagami, a bored top student, finds a notebook dropped by the death god Ryuk: anyone whose name is written in it dies. He sets out to rid the world of criminals by killing them, drawing a worldwide police hunt led by the eccentric detective L, and the story becomes a battle of wits between them (VIZ blurb via AniList; ANN review of volume 1).
entry.life_message: Power to judge who deserves to die corrupts the one who takes it; justice belongs to accountable law, not one person's will (to verify how the ending frames it).

content.note: Killings by notebook drive the plot; ANN says they are not shown in graphic detail; MU Serial Killer/s, Death; AniList Crime, Tragedy.
ANN calls it possibly too dark for some, with a grotesque death god and gallows humor; AniList Tragedy (92), Gods.
Nothing sexual noted in the sources opened (to verify).
ANN mentions no strong language (to verify).
None noted.
Protagonist described as megalomaniac and sociopathic (MU); memory manipulation (AniList); no self-harm noted (to verify).
Writing names to 'kill' and deceiving family and police are central (MU Manipulative Protagonist, Deception) (to verify).
None noted.

entry.dominant: Utilitarian vigilantism critiqued; might makes right; bleak view of death

frames.aligns: Shows how claiming God's power over life breeds pride; dignity of even criminals' lives at stake.
frames.concerns: Death god and notebook as occult tool; murder-as-justice debated without clear answer early on.

frames.aligns: A study of pride and the passions consuming a gifted young man.
frames.concerns: Ryuk as an attractive death spirit; prolonged immersion in a killer's mind feeds the passions.

frames.aligns: Light's 'new world' is shown as ego, not righteousness (ANN).
frames.concerns: Shinigami gods and supernatural killing; deceptive anti-hero readers may admire.

frames.aligns: Strong discussion starter on who may judge and why vengeance is not ours.
frames.concerns: Ryuk and death-god rules; Light's cleverness can make sin look appealing.

frames.aligns: Exposes the corruption of playing God.
frames.concerns: A demon-like death god partners with a teen; spiritual power used for killing.

frames.aligns: Portrays sin's self-deceit truthfully; the magistrate's sword versus private vengeance.
frames.concerns: Gods of death as a false cosmology; little to no grace offered.

frames.aligns: Two-kingdoms question: lawful authority versus a self-appointed judge.
frames.concerns: Fifth-commandment violations made into a thrilling game.

frames.aligns: Moral seriousness about murder and pride.
frames.concerns: Hard to read in the name of the Lord; dark immersion in killing.

frames.aligns: A morality tale judged by how it frames good and evil; ego shown as ruin.
frames.concerns: Ambiguous early framing lets readers cheer Kira.

frames.aligns: Questions state and private violence alike.
frames.concerns: Killing as problem-solving at the story's core; worldly thriller.

frames.aligns: Agency and its abuse are central; honesty versus Light's lies.
frames.concerns: Dark, death-saturated content; not clearly 'virtuous, lovely'.
Capital punishment logic explored without clear resolution in early volumes.

frames.aligns: Only God decrees death; Light's claim to judge shown as arrogance.
frames.concerns: Death gods as real beings (shirk concern); magic-like power over life.

frames.aligns: Karma-like consequences of adharma and ego.
frames.concerns: Tamasic absorption in killing and deceit.

frames.aligns: Shows craving for power and righteous anger producing suffering.
frames.concerns: First precept broken repeatedly; deceit as strategy.

frames.aligns: Questions extrajudicial killing and unchecked state-like power.
frames.concerns: Almost all-male cast; idealized genius villain.

frames.aligns: Rigorous ethics debate on punishment, rights and reason; ANN praises its moral questions.
frames.concerns: Supernatural rules are fiction only; little to raise.

frames.aligns: Police and lawful order oppose a self-made tyrant.
frames.concerns: Charismatic anti-hero may be admired by teens; moral relativism early on.

frames.aligns: Pride's downfall is a biblical theme.
frames.concerns: Death gods and spirit beings; 'by beholding' a killer's mind for 12 volumes.
Death god and spiritistic power; violence central (Psalm 11:5).

frames.aligns: Fear and death as mental tyranny, broken by truth-seeking L.
frames.concerns: Dwelling on death and fear-inducing images.

frames.aligns: Invites free inquiry on justice and the worth of every person.
Power used to harm returns on the user, a threefold-law echo.
frames.concerns: Manipulative magic-like power at the center.

frames.aligns: Shinigami as familiar supernatural figures; sincerity versus Light's two faces.
Ego (haumai) destroys; justice is God's, not one man's.
frames.concerns: Light kills the helpless, not defending the oppressed.

frames.aligns: Truthfulness and lawful order versus deception.
'Do not murder' and trustworthiness tested and shown to matter.
Individual will against authority; rational strategy.
frames.concerns: Light's arbitrary authority over life is the tyranny Satanic Temple rejects.

frames.aligns: Judgment belongs to God and lawful courts; Light usurps both.
frames.concerns: Sorcery-like death power; heavy bittul Torah dark entertainment.

frames.aligns: Law, due process and tikkun olam versus vigilante 'justice'.
Ethical dilemma on punishment and power suited to discussion.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Rivalry of pride between Light and L, but disputes run through investigation, not personal duels (ANN).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Police and law are the counterweight to Light; Light himself seeks an imposed moral order (MU World Domination).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Light deceives his police-chief father; justice for all over family (MU blurb).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Light wants to rule as a god over a purified world (MU Megalomania).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Strategy, deduction and rules of the notebook dominate; shinigami are rule-bound, not worshipped.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Security from crime is the stated goal of Kira's killings.

folkways.japan: Japan's National Police Agency and a strong cultural respect for public order frame the hunt for Kira, and capital punishment's place in Japanese law sits behind the debate.

delivery.evidence: ANN says the volume raises questions about murder and whose lives matter without answering them.

personified.ideology: Utilitarian vigilante justice; ends justify killing
Rule of law and due process by deduction

delivery.note: The argument for and against Kira is carried by the duel of minds rather than speeches, with Light's growing ego the main signal (ANN).

entry.winners_losers: Through most volumes Light and L trade victories; criminals and anyone in Light's way lose their lives. The VIZ blurb and ANN frame Light's ego as his undoing, so sympathy leans to lawful justice (ending to verify).

Whether any deaths are drawn graphically in later volumes
